# Existence of multisoliton solutions of the gravitational Hartree equation in three dimensions

**Authors:** Yutong Wu Address: Department of Mathematics, Yale University, New Haven, CT 06511 Email address: yutong.wu.yw894@yale.edu

## Abstract

We prove the existence of multisoliton solutions of the three-dimensional gravitational Hartree equation whose trajectories follow many body dynamics of hyperbolic, parabolic or hyperbolic-parabolic types. This work generalizes and improves the result of Krieger-Martel-Raphaël [8] on two-soliton solutions.

## 1. Introduction

### 1.1. Background

In 1927, soon after the Schrödinger equation was proposed, Douglas Hartree derived the Hartree equation, which provided a way to study many body quantum systems. It has then attracted the interest of both physicists and mathematicians.

In this paper, we consider the gravitational Hartree equation in 3D

$$ iu_{t}+\Delta u-\phi_{|u|^{2}}u=0, $$

where $u:\mathbb{R}\times\mathbb{R}^{3}\to\mathbb{C}$ and

$$ \phi_{|u|^{2}}=\Delta^{-1}(|u|^{2})=-\frac{1}{4\pi|x|}*|u|^{2}. $$

We begin with some properties of the equation.

The equation possesses a large family of symmetries. Namely, if $u$ solves (1.1), then for any $(t_{0},\alpha_{0},\beta_{0},\lambda_{0},\gamma_{0})\in\mathbb{R}\times\mathbb{R}^{3}\times\mathbb{R}^{3}\times\mathbb{R}_{+}\times(\mathbb{R}/2\pi\mathbb{Z})$ ,

$$ v(t,x)=\lambda_{0}^{2}u(\lambda_{0}^{2}t+t_{0},\lambda_{0}x-\alpha_{0}-\beta_{0}t)e^{i(\frac{1}{2}\beta_{0}\cdot x-\frac{1}{4}|\beta_{0}|^{2}t+\gamma_{0})} $$

also solves (1.1). In view of Noether’s theorem, we expect the equation to have some conservation laws. The following quantities are conserved by the equation:

$$ \displaystyle\mathcal{M}(u)=\int|u(t,x)|^{2}\mathrm{d}x, \displaystyle\mathcal{P}(u)=\int\mathrm{Im}\big(\nabla u(t,x)\overline{u(t,x)}\big)\mathrm{d}x, \displaystyle\mathcal{H}(u)=\frac{1}{2}\int|\nabla u(t,x)|^{2}\mathrm{d}x-\frac{1}{4}\int\big|\nabla\phi_{|u|^{2}}(t,x)\big|^{2}\mathrm{d}x, $$

In other words, if $u$ solves (1.1), then these quantities are independent of $t$ .

The equation (1.1) is mass ( $L^{2}$ )-subcritical. By Theorem 6.1.1 in [1], we know the Cauchy problem of (1.1) is globally wellposed in $H^{1}$ . To be more precise, for any $u_{0}\in H^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{3})$ , there exists a unique $u\in C\big(\mathbb{R};H^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{3})\big)$ satisfying (1.1) and $u(0,x)=u_{0}(x)$ . Moreover, this $u$ depends on $u_{0}$ continuously.

The linear Schrödinger equation $iu_{t}+\Delta u=0$ is called dispersive because of the dispersive estimate $\|e^{it\Delta}f\|_{L^{\infty}}\lesssim t^{-\frac{3}{2}}\|f\|_{L^{1}}$ for any $f\in L^{1}\cap L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{3}),\ t>0$ . However, due to the (focusing) nonlinearity, there exist non-dispersive solutions to (1.1) called solitary waves.

A solitary wave is a solution to (1.1) of the form $u(t,x)=e^{it}W(x)$ . We deduce that $W$ satisfies $\Delta W-\phi_{|W|^{2}}W=W$ . From [10] we know there exists a unique radial and nonnegative solution $Q$ of

$$ \Delta Q-\phi_{Q^{2}}Q=Q, $$

called the ground state. It is proved in [11] that this $Q$ can also be characterized as the radial minimizer of the Hamiltonian subject to a given $L^{2}$ norm. More precisely, it minimizes

$$ \mathcal{H}(u)=\frac{1}{2}\int|\nabla u|^{2}-\frac{1}{4}\int|\nabla\phi_{|u|^{2}}|^{2}, $$

among all $u\in H^{1}$ with the same $L^{2}$ norm as $Q$ . Another property of $Q$ is the exponential decay:

$$ Q(x)\leq Ce^{-c|x|},\quad\forall x\in\mathbb{R}^{3}. $$

Using (1.3) we can construct a family of ground state solitary waves.

The main object of interest in this paper is the multisolitary wave, or multisoliton, which can be roughly understood as the sum of several solitary waves.

Multisolitary waves are expected to be important components of generic solutions as claimed in the soliton resolution conjecture. It plays an crucial role when we try to understand the long time behavior of solutions. We cite [23], [21], [22], [6], [5] and [3] as references for some partial results on soliton resolution for some nonlinear dispersive equations. Another aspect is to study the existence and stability of solutions that approach given multisolitons. In this direction, [16], [17] and [4] proved the existence of solutions that asymptotically approach multisoliton with constant and distinct speeds for the nonlinear Schrödinger equation (NLS), the generalized Korteweg-de Vries equation (gKdV) and the nonlinear Klein Gordon equation (NLKG), respectively. Moreover, [7] and [15] studied the stability of such multisoliton solutions. The general expectation is that multisolitons are orbitally stable if the speeds are separated.

We point out that the above literature only considered equations with local nonlinearity. For such equations, the sum of two ground state solitary waves moving away at a constant speed solves the equation up to a term that decays exponentially in time. This reflects that the nonlinearity does not affect the asymptotic behavior dramatically. On the other hand, the long time behavior of the Hartree equation is difficult to study because of the long range effect of the nonlinearity. More precisely, we have

$$ \phi_{Q^{2}}(x)\sim\frac{1}{|x|}\quad\text{as }x\to\infty, $$

where $\sim$ means comparable up to constants, so the error term at most admits a polynomial decay. A quantitative estimate of such errors is given in Lemma 2.5. This is the main difficulty we have to deal with.

### 1.2. The m-body problem

As a starting point of the study of long time dynamics, Krieger, Martel and Raphaël [8] studied the existence of two-soliton solutions of (1.1). This pioneer paper revealed that one should expect a gravitational two-body interaction within the two solitons. This interaction cancels the long range effect properly. In this subsection, we review some important facts about the $m$ -body problem.

Let $m\geq 2$ . The $\mathbf{m}$ -body problem is an ODE system

$$ \dot{\alpha}_{j}(t)=2\beta_{j}(t),\quad\dot{\beta}_{j}(t)=-\sum_{k\neq j}\frac{\|Q\|_{L^{2}}^{2}}{4\pi\lambda_{k}}\cdot\frac{\alpha_{j}(t)-\alpha_{k}(t)}{\left|\alpha_{j}(t)-\alpha_{k}(t)\right|^{3}},\qquad\forall 1\leq j\leq m, $$

where $\alpha_{j},\beta_{j}\in C^{1}\big(\mathbb{R},\mathbb{R}^{3}\big)$ and $\lambda_{j}\in\mathbb{R}_{+}$ for $1\leq j\leq m$ .

The case where $m=2$ is the famous two-body problem. It is known that the solution to the two-body problem is hyperbolic, parabolic or elliptic, corresponding to the asymptotic behavior being

$$ |\alpha_{1}(t)-\alpha_{2}(t)|\sim t^{q}\text{ as }t\to+\infty $$

with $q=1$ , $q=\frac{2}{3}$ or $q=0$ , respectively. In this paper, we write $f\sim g$ if there exist $0<c<C$ such that $cf\leq g\leq Cf$ .

The $m$ -body problem for $m\geq 3$ , as opposed to the two-body problem, is much more complicated. Even for three-body, chaotic dynamics may occur [19]. For our purpose, we will focus on expansive solutions, which means $|\alpha_{j}(t)-\alpha_{k}(t)|\to+\infty$ as $t\to+\infty$ for any $j\neq k$ . On the PDE side, this requires the centers of solitons to move far away from each other, which is essential for us to exploit the exponential decay of the ground state (1.6).

By translation we may set the center of the system at the origin. Consider the following sets of configurations

$$ \displaystyle\mathcal{X}=\Big\{(x_{1},\cdots,x_{m})\in\mathbb{R}^{3m}\ \Big|\ \sum_{j=1}^{m}\lambda_{j}^{-1}x_{j}=0\Big\}, \displaystyle\mathcal{Y}=\big\{(x_{1},\cdots,x_{m})\in\mathcal{X}\ \big|\ x_{j}\neq x_{k},\ \forall j\neq k\big\}\quad\text{and}\quad\Delta=\mathcal{X}\setminus\mathcal{Y}. $$

The final evolution of expansive solutions is described as follows.

#### Theorem (Marchal-Saari [14]).

For an expansive solution of (1.8) centered at the origin, there exists $(a_{1},\cdots,a_{m})\in\mathcal{X}$ such that

$$ \alpha_{j}=a_{j}t+O(t^{\frac{2}{3}}),\ 1\leq j\leq m\quad\text{as }t\to+\infty. $$

Moreover, if $a_{j}=a_{k}$ for some $j\neq k$ , then $|\alpha_{j}-\alpha_{k}|\sim t^{\frac{2}{3}}$ as $t\to+\infty$ .

We classify solutions of the form (1.10) into the following three types in the spirit of Chazy [2] according to the growth of distances between different bodies.

- • hyperbolic: $(a_{1},\cdots,a_{m})\in\mathcal{Y}$ , or equivalently, for all $j\neq k$ , (1.11)

$$ |\alpha_{j}(t)-\alpha_{k}(t)|\sim t\quad\text{as }t\to+\infty. $$

- • parabolic: $(a_{1},\cdots,a_{m})=0$ , or equivalently, for all $j\neq k$ , (1.12)

$$ |\alpha_{j}(t)-\alpha_{k}(t)|\sim t^{\frac{2}{3}}\quad\text{as }t\to+\infty. $$

- • hyperbolic-parabolic: $(a_{1},\cdots,a_{m})\in\Delta\setminus\{0\}$ . In this case, both of the above pairwise asymptotics occur, and they are the only possibilities.

Notice that this agrees with the previous notion for two-body dynamics, where the hyperbolic-parabolic dynamic does not appear evidently.

The existence of such three types of solutions has been studied in the recent years. The newest results in this direction are obtained through a variational approach originating from Maderna-Venturelli [13]. See also [12] for a similar strategy. We state the results as follows.

#### Theorem (Maderna-Venturelli [13]; Polimeni-Terracini [20]).

Let $\lambda_{j}\in\mathbb{R}_{+}$ for $1\leq j\leq m$ .

- (1) There exists a hyperbolic solution to (1.8) of the form (1.13)

$$ \alpha_{j}(t)=a_{j}t+O(\log t)\quad\text{as }t\to+\infty $$

for any $(a_{1},\cdots,a_{m})\in\mathcal{Y}$ and initial configuration in $\mathcal{X}$ .

- (2) There exists a parabolic solution to (1.8) of the form (1.14)

$$ \alpha_{j}(t)=cb_{j}t^{\frac{2}{3}}+o(t^{\frac{1}{3}+})\quad\text{as }t\to+\infty $$

for any minimal $(b_{1},\cdots,b_{m})\in\mathcal{Y}$ and initial configuration in $\mathcal{X}$ , where $c>0$ is determined by $b_{1},\cdots,b_{m}$ .

- (3) There exists a hyperbolic-parabolic solution to (1.8) of the form (1.15)

$$ \alpha_{j}(t)=a_{j}t+c_{j}b_{j}t^{\frac{2}{3}}+o(t^{\frac{1}{3}+})\quad\text{as }t\to+\infty $$

for any $(a_{1},\cdots,a_{m})\in\Delta\setminus\{0\}$ , minimal $(b_{1},\cdots,b_{m})\in\mathcal{Y}$ and initial configuration in $\mathcal{X}$ , where $c_{j}>0$ is determined by $a_{1},\cdots,a_{m},b_{1},\cdots,b_{m}$ and $c_{j}=c_{k}$ whenever $a_{j}=a_{k}$ .

Regarding the term minimal, see Remark 2 after Theorem 1.

### 1.3. The main result

The result in [8] is that for the two-body problem, hyperbolic and parabolic solutions to (1.8) produce two-soliton solutions of (1.1). Based on their method, we generalize their result to $m$ -soliton solutions. Our result asserts the existence of multisoliton solutions to (1.1) reproducing the above three expansive dynamics. An assumption on the masses is needed for the last two dynamics.

#### Theorem 1.

Let $(\alpha_{1}^{\infty},\cdots,\alpha_{m}^{\infty},\beta_{1}^{\infty},\cdots,\beta_{m}^{\infty},\lambda_{1}^{\infty},\cdots,\lambda_{m}^{\infty})$ be a solution to (1.8) of one of the three types (1.13), (1.14) or (1.15). Suppose $\lambda_{j}^{\infty}=\lambda_{k}^{\infty}$ whenever $|\alpha_{j}^{\infty}(t)-\alpha_{k}^{\infty}(t)|\sim t^{\frac{2}{3}}$ as $t\to+\infty$ .

Then there exists a solution $u$ to (1.1) and $\gamma_{1}^{\infty}(t),\cdots\gamma_{m}^{\infty}(t)$ that are $C^{1}$ in $t$ such that

$$ \lim_{t\to+\infty}\bigg\|u(t,x)-\sum_{j=1}^{m}\frac{1}{(\lambda_{j}^{\infty})^{2}}Q\Big(\frac{x-\alpha_{j}^{\infty}(t)}{\lambda_{j}^{\infty}}\Big)e^{-i\gamma_{j}^{\infty}(t)+i\beta_{j}^{\infty}(t)\cdot x}\bigg\|_{H^{1}}=0. $$

#### Remark.

1. In the parabolic case, Theorem 1 improves the result in [8] as we take $\alpha_{j}$ (in their statement) to be identical to $\alpha_{j}^{\infty}$ , which trivially answers their Comment 2.

2. The assumption that $(b_{1},\cdots,b_{m})$ is minimal in (1.14) and (1.15) is not directly used when we deal with the parabolic case and the hyperbolic-parabolic case. The precise definition of “minimal” can be found in [20], and this assumption is needed there to guarantee the existence of solutions of the $m$ -body problem. Note also that this refers to different properties in (1.14) and (1.15).

3. Our result seems a satisfactory counterpart of [16] and [17], which dealt with the existence of multisolitary waves of (NLS) and (gKdV), respectively. Moreover, by [18], a radiation term is not expected for multisoliton solutions of the Hartree equation. Thus in the spirit of the soliton resolution conjecture, we have constructed a relatively complete class of solutions.

4. Some future problems related to this work include the following: Are the multisoliton solutions constructed above stable? Do multisoliton solutions with elliptic type interactions exist? Can the results be extended to other dimensions?

Using the expansion of hyperbolic motions given by Chazy [2], for any $(x_{1},\cdots,x_{m})\in\mathcal{X}$ and $(a_{1},\cdots,a_{m})\in\mathcal{Y}$ , there exists a solution to (1.8) of the form $\alpha_{j}(t)=x_{j}+a_{j}t+c_{j}\log t+o(1)$ for some $(c_{1},\cdots,c_{m})\in\mathcal{X}$ . Then we deduce the following from Theorem 1.

#### Corollary 2.

Given $\lambda_{1},\cdots,\lambda_{m}\in\mathbb{R}_{+}$ , $x_{1},\cdots,x_{m}\in\mathbb{R}^{3}$ and distinct $a_{1},\cdots,a_{m}\in\mathbb{R}^{3}$ , there exist $c_{1},\cdots,c_{m}\in\mathbb{R}^{3}$ , a solution $u$ to (1.1), and $\gamma_{1}(t),\cdots\gamma_{m}(t)$ that are $C^{1}$ in $t$ such that

$$ \lim_{t\to+\infty}\bigg\|u(t,x)-\sum_{j=1}^{m}\frac{1}{\lambda_{j}^{2}}Q\Big(\frac{x-x_{j}-a_{j}t-c_{j}\log t}{\lambda_{j}}\Big)e^{-i\gamma_{j}(t)+i\frac{a_{j}}{2}\cdot x}\bigg\|_{H^{1}}=0. $$

#### Remark.

Comparing Corollary 2 with the results in [16] and [17], we see that the $c_{j}\log t$ term is the necessary corrector accounting for the long range effect of the Hartree nonlinearity.

We end the introduction section with some comments on the proof of the theorem and the organization of the paper.

Due to the long range effect mentioned before, we need to first construct approximate solutions. The difficulty compared to [8] lies mainly in the parabolic and hyperbolic-parabolic cases. We need to study an approximate system of the $m$ -body problem, which is essentially harder than the two-body case. For this purpose, we have to perform delicate computation of the constants involved. We made use of a cancellation of errors displayed in the proof of Proposition 5.1. This is a new observation.

The article is organized as follows. In Section 2, we construct approximate multisolitary solutions of (1.1) up to the $N$ -th order for any $N\geq 1$ to overcome the long range effect. We then focus on the hyperbolic case. We reduce the problem to a uniform estimate and furthermore a modulation estimate in Section 3. Then the modulation estimate is proved in Section 4, finishing the proof of the hyperbolic case. The other two cases of Theorem 1 are addressed in section 5.

## 2. Approximate solutions

First we introduce some notations. For $\alpha_{j}$ , $\beta_{j}$ , $\lambda_{j}$ and $\gamma_{j}$ (may depending on time), we denote

$$ \begin{gathered}\alpha=(\alpha_{1},\cdots,\alpha_{m}),\quad\beta=(\beta_{1},\cdots,\beta_{m}),\\
\lambda=(\lambda_{1},\cdots,\lambda_{m}),\quad\gamma=(\gamma_{1},\cdots,\gamma_{m}),\\
P=(\alpha,\beta,\lambda),\quad g=(P,\gamma),\quad g_{j}=(\alpha_{j},\beta_{j},\lambda_{j},\gamma_{j}),\\
\alpha_{jk}=\alpha_{j}-\alpha_{k},\quad\beta_{jk}=\beta_{j}-\beta_{k},\quad a=\min_{j\neq k}|\alpha_{jk}|.\end{gathered} $$

We use similar notation when there are superscripts.

For $u:\mathbb{R}\times\mathbb{R}^{3}\to\mathbb{C}$ , we define $g_{j}u:\mathbb{R}\times\mathbb{R}^{3}\to\mathbb{C}$ by

$$ \begin{gathered}g_{j}u(t,x)=\frac{1}{\lambda_{j}^{2}}u\Big(t,\frac{x-\alpha_{j}}{\lambda_{j}}\Big)e^{-i\gamma_{j}+i\beta_{j}\cdot x}.\end{gathered} $$

In particular, $g_{j}Q$ represents a soliton and $\sum\limits_{j=1}^{m}g_{j}Q$ is a multisoliton.

Assume $u=g_{j}v$ and the components of $g_{j}$ may depend on $t$ . More precisely, we assume

$$ u(t,x)=\frac{1}{\lambda_{j}^{2}(t)}v\left(t,\frac{x-\alpha_{j}(t)}{\lambda_{j}(t)}\right)e^{-i\gamma_{j}(t)+i\beta_{j}(t)\cdot x}. $$

Then we have

$$ \displaystyle u_{t}=\frac{1}{\lambda_{j}^{4}}\Big(\lambda_{j}^{2}v_{t}-\lambda_{j}\dot{\alpha}_{j}\cdot\nabla v-\dot{\lambda}_{j}(x-\alpha_{j})\cdot\nabla v-2\lambda_{j}\dot{\lambda}_{j}v \displaystyle-i\lambda_{j}^{2}\dot{\gamma}_{j}v+i\lambda_{j}^{2}\dot{\beta}_{j}\cdot xv\Big)e^{-i\gamma_{j}+i\beta_{j}\cdot x}, \displaystyle\nabla u=\frac{1}{\lambda_{j}^{3}}\left(\nabla v+i\lambda_{j}\beta_{j}v\right)e^{-i\gamma_{j}+i\beta_{j}\cdot x}, \displaystyle\Delta u=\frac{1}{\lambda_{j}^{4}}\left(\Delta v+2i\lambda_{j}\beta_{j}\cdot\nabla v-\lambda_{j}^{2}|\beta_{j}|^{2}v\right)e^{-i\gamma_{j}+i\beta_{j}\cdot x}, \displaystyle\phi_{|u|^{2}}(x)=\frac{1}{\lambda_{j}^{2}}\phi_{|v|^{2}}\Big(\frac{x-\alpha_{j}}{\lambda_{j}}\Big). $$

Therefore, if we let

$$ u(t,x):=\sum_{j=1}^{m}u_{j}(t,x):=\sum_{j=1}^{m}g_{j}v_{j}(t,x), $$

and set $y_{j}=\frac{x-\alpha_{j}(t)}{\lambda_{j}(t)}$ , $\Lambda v_{j}=2v_{j}+y_{j}\cdot\nabla v_{j}$ , then

$$ iu_{t}+\Delta u-\phi_{|u^{2}|}u=\sum_{j=1}^{m}\frac{1}{\lambda_{j}^{4}}E_{j}(t,y_{j})e^{-i\gamma_{j}+i\beta_{j}\cdot x}-\sum_{k\neq j}\phi_{\mathrm{Re}(u_{k}\overline{u_{j}})}u, $$

where

$$ \displaystyle E_{j}(t,y_{j})= \displaystyle i\lambda_{j}^{2}\partial_{t}v_{j}+\Delta v_{j}-v_{j}-i\lambda_{j}\dot{\lambda}_{j}\Lambda v_{j}-\lambda_{j}^{3}\dot{\beta}_{j}\cdot y_{j}v_{j} \displaystyle-i\lambda_{j}\left(\dot{\alpha}_{j}-2\beta_{j}\right)\nabla v_{j}+\lambda_{j}^{2}\left(\dot{\gamma}_{j}+\frac{1}{\lambda_{j}^{2}}-|\beta_{j}|^{2}-\dot{\beta}_{j}\cdot\alpha_{j}\right)v_{j} \displaystyle-\left[\phi_{|v_{j}|^{2}}+\sum_{k\neq j}\left(\frac{\lambda_{j}}{\lambda_{k}}\right)^{2}\phi_{|v_{k}|^{2}}\left(t,\frac{\lambda_{j}}{\lambda_{k}}y_{j}+\frac{\alpha_{jk}}{\lambda_{k}}\right)\right]v_{j}. $$

To be clear, the space variable of the right hand side is $y_{j}$ unless explicitly written out.

### 2.1. Definition of approximate solutions

We need to approximate the last term of $E_{j}$ . Since

$$ \left(\frac{\lambda_{j}}{\lambda_{k}}\right)^{2}\phi_{|v_{k}|^{2}}\left(t,\frac{\lambda_{j}}{\lambda_{k}}y_{j}+\frac{\alpha_{jk}}{\lambda_{k}}\right)=-\frac{\lambda_{j}^{2}}{4\pi\lambda_{k}}\int_{\mathbb{R}^{3}}\frac{|v_{k}(t,\xi)|^{2}}{|\lambda_{j}y_{j}+\alpha_{jk}-\lambda_{k}\xi|}\mathrm{d}\xi, $$

we consider the Taylor expansion

$$ \frac{1}{|\alpha-\zeta|}=\sum_{n=1}^{N}F_{n}(\alpha,\zeta)+O\left(\frac{|\zeta|^{N}}{|\alpha|^{N+1}}\right)\quad\text{as }\zeta\to 0, $$

where $F_{n}(\alpha,\zeta)$ is homogeneous of degree $-n$ in $\alpha$ and of degree $n-1$ in $\zeta$ . We define the approximation to be

$$ \displaystyle\phi_{|v_{k}|^{2}}^{(N)}(t,y_{j}) \displaystyle:=\sum_{n=1}^{N}\psi_{|v_{k}|^{2}}^{(n)}(t,y_{j}) \displaystyle:=\sum_{n=1}^{N}-\frac{\lambda_{j}^{2}}{4\pi\lambda_{k}}\int_{\mathbb{R}^{3}}|v_{k}(t,\xi)|^{2}F_{n}(\alpha_{jk},\lambda_{k}\xi-\lambda_{j}y_{j})\mathrm{d}\xi. $$

Explicit formulae for the first few terms are as follows:

$$ \displaystyle\psi_{|v_{k}|^{2}}^{(1)}(t,y_{j})=-\frac{\lambda_{j}^{2}}{4\pi\lambda_{k}|\alpha_{jk}|}\int|v_{k}(t,\xi)|^{2}\mathrm{d}\xi, \displaystyle\psi_{|v_{k}|^{2}}^{(2)}(t,y_{j})=-\frac{\lambda_{j}^{2}}{4\pi\lambda_{k}|\alpha_{jk}|^{3}}\int\Big(\lambda_{k}(\alpha_{jk}\cdot\xi)|v_{k}(t,\xi)|^{2}-\lambda_{j}(y_{j}\cdot\alpha_{jk})|v_{k}(t,\xi)|^{2}\Big)\mathrm{d}\xi. $$

We will need to take $v_{k}=Q$ . In this case we denote $\psi_{|v_{k}|^{2}}^{(n)}$ by $\psi_{Q^{2},k}^{(n)}$ . Namely,

$$ \psi_{Q^{2},k}^{(n)}(y_{j})=-\frac{\lambda_{j}^{2}}{4\pi\lambda_{k}}\int_{\mathbb{R}^{3}}Q^{2}(\xi)F_{n}(\alpha_{jk},\lambda_{k}\xi-\lambda_{j}y_{j})\mathrm{d}\xi. $$

We shall let $v_{j}$ vary in $N$ , and we also assume $v_{j}$ depends on time only through the parameters $t\mapsto P(t)$ , which means $v_{j}(t,y_{j})=V_{j}^{(N)}(P(t),y_{j})$ for some $V_{j}^{(N)}$ .

Define

$$ \displaystyle R_{g}^{(N)}(t,x):=\sum_{j=1}^{m}R_{j,g}^{(N)}(t,x):=\sum_{j=1}^{m}g_{j}V_{j}^{(N)}(P(t),x). $$

Let us omit the subscript $g$ of $R^{(N)}$ for now. We have

$$ \displaystyle i\partial_{t}R^{(N)}+\Delta R^{(N)}-\phi_{|R^{(N)}|^{2}}R^{(N)} \displaystyle= \displaystyle\sum_{j=1}^{m}\frac{1}{\lambda_{j}^{4}}E_{j}^{(N)}(t,y_{j})e^{-i\gamma_{j}+i\beta_{j}\cdot x}-\sum_{k\neq j}\phi_{\mathrm{Re}(R_{k}^{(N)}\overline{R_{j}^{(N)}})}R^{(N)} \displaystyle+\sum_{j=1}^{m}\frac{1}{\lambda_{j}^{4}}\sum_{k\neq j}\left[\phi_{\left|V_{k}^{(N)}\right|^{2}}^{(N)}-\left(\frac{\lambda_{j}}{\lambda_{k}}\right)^{2}\phi_{|V_{k}^{(N)}|^{2}}\left(P(t),\frac{\lambda_{j}}{\lambda_{k}}y_{j}+\frac{\alpha_{jk}}{\lambda_{k}}\right)\right]V_{j}^{(N)}e^{-i\gamma_{j}+i\beta_{j}\cdot x}, $$

where

$$ \displaystyle E_{j}^{(N)}= \displaystyle i\lambda_{j}^{2}\partial_{t}V_{j}^{(N)}+\Delta V_{j}^{(N)}-V_{j}^{(N)}-i\lambda_{j}\dot{\lambda}_{j}\Lambda V_{j}^{(N)}-\lambda_{j}^{3}\dot{\beta}_{j}\cdot y_{j}V_{j}^{(N)} \displaystyle-i\lambda_{j}\left(\dot{\alpha}_{j}-2\beta_{j}\right)\nabla V_{j}^{(N)}+\lambda_{j}^{2}\left(\dot{\gamma}_{j}+\frac{1}{\lambda_{j}^{2}}-|\beta_{j}|^{2}-\dot{\beta}_{j}\cdot\alpha_{j}\right)V_{j}^{(N)} \displaystyle-\left(\phi_{\left|V_{j}^{(N)}\right|^{2}}+\sum_{k\neq j}\phi_{\left|V_{k}^{(N)}\right|^{2}}^{(N)}\right)V_{j}^{(N)}. $$

For functions $M_{j}^{(N)}(P)$ and $B_{j}^{(N)}(P)$ of the parameters, we can decompose

$$ E_{j}^{(N)}=\tilde{E}_{j}^{(N)}+S_{j}^{(N)}, $$

where

$$ \displaystyle\tilde{E}_{j}^{(N)}(t,y_{j})= \displaystyle\Delta V_{j}^{(N)}-V_{j}^{(N)}-\phi_{\left|V_{j}^{(N)}\right|^{2}}V_{j}^{(N)}-\sum_{k\neq j}\phi_{\left|V_{k}^{(N)}\right|^{2}}^{(N)}V_{j}^{(N)} \displaystyle-i\lambda_{j}M_{j}^{(N)}\Lambda V_{j}^{(N)}-\lambda_{j}^{3}B_{j}^{(N)}\cdot y_{j}V_{j}^{(N)} \displaystyle+i\lambda_{j}^{2}\sum_{k=1}^{m}\bigg(\frac{\partial V_{j}^{(N)}}{\partial\alpha_{k}}\cdot 2\beta_{k}+\frac{\partial V_{j}^{(N)}}{\partial\beta_{k}}\cdot B_{k}^{(N)}+\frac{\partial V_{j}^{(N)}}{\partial\lambda_{k}}M_{k}^{(N)}\bigg) $$

and

$$ \displaystyle S_{j}^{(N)}(t,x)= \displaystyle-i\lambda_{j}\left(\dot{\alpha}_{j}-2\beta_{j}\right)\nabla V_{j}^{(N)}-\lambda_{j}^{3}\left(\dot{\beta}_{j}-B_{j}^{(N)}\right)\cdot y_{j}V_{j}^{(N)} \displaystyle-i\lambda_{j}\left(\dot{\lambda}_{j}-M_{j}^{(N)}\right)\Lambda V_{j}^{(N)}+\lambda_{j}^{2}\bigg(\dot{\gamma}_{j}+\frac{1}{\lambda_{j}^{2}}-|\beta_{j}|^{2}-\dot{\beta}_{j}\cdot\alpha_{j}\bigg)V_{j}^{(N)} \displaystyle+i\lambda_{j}^{2}\sum_{k=1}^{m}\Bigg[\frac{\partial V_{j}^{(N)}}{\partial\alpha_{k}}\cdot\left(\dot{\alpha}_{k}-2\beta_{k}\right)+\frac{\partial V_{j}^{(N)}}{\partial\beta_{k}}\cdot\left(\dot{\beta}_{k}-B_{k}^{(N)}\right) \displaystyle+\frac{\partial V_{j}^{(N)}}{\partial\lambda_{k}}\left(\dot{\lambda}_{k}-M_{k}^{(N)}\right)\Bigg]. $$

Note that $\tilde{E}_{j}^{(N)}$ is set to be a function of $y_{j}$ instead of $x$ . This is to align with a later statement. It does not matter whether $S_{j}^{(N)}$ is a function of $y_{j}$ or $x$ , but we will let it be a function of $x$ for preciseness.

We remark that $\tilde{E}_{j}^{(N)}$ accounts for the error terms arising from the nonlinearity, while $S_{j}^{(N)}$ contains the error terms caused by the parameters. We introduce $M_{j}^{(N)}$ and $B_{j}^{(N)}$ to provide flexibility in controlling $\tilde{E}_{j}^{(N)}$ .

Next, we show that we can choose $V_{j}^{(N)}$ , $M_{j}^{(N)}$ , and $B_{j}^{(N)}$ so that $\tilde{E}_{j}^{(N)}$ is small. This smallness will be a result of homogeneity, so we give the following definition.

#### Definition 2.1 (Admissible functions).

Recalling (2.1), let $\Omega$ denote the space of non-collision positions:

$$ \displaystyle\Omega:=\Big\{P=(\alpha,\beta,\lambda)\in\mathbb{R}^{3m}\times\mathbb{R}^{3m}\times\mathbb{R}_{+}^{m}\ \big|\ \alpha_{j}\neq\alpha_{k},\ \forall j\neq k\Big\}. $$

(1) Let $n\in\mathbb{N}$ . Define $S_{n}$ to be the set of functions $\sigma:\Omega\to\mathbb{C}$ that is homogeneous in $\alpha$ of degree $-n$ and is a finite sum of

$$ c\prod_{j\neq k}(\alpha_{j}-\alpha_{k})^{p_{jk}}|\alpha_{j}-\alpha_{k}|^{-q_{jk}}\prod_{j=1}^{m}\beta_{j}^{k_{j}}\lambda_{j}^{l_{j}}, $$

where $c\in\mathbb{C}$ , $p_{jk}\in\mathbb{N}^{3}$ , $q_{jk}\in\mathbb{N}$ , $k_{j}\in\mathbb{N}^{3}$ , $l_{j}\in\mathbb{Z}$ and $|p_{jk}|\leq q_{jk}$ .

(2) We say a function $u:\Omega\times\mathbb{R}^{3}\to\mathbb{C}$ is admissible if $u$ is a finite sum of

$$ \sigma(\alpha_{1},\cdots,\alpha_{m},\beta_{1},\cdots,\beta_{m},\lambda_{1},\cdots\lambda_{m})\tau(x), $$

where $\sigma\in S_{n}$ for some $n\in\mathbb{N}$ and $\tau\in C^{\infty}$ satisfies

$$ \big|\nabla^{k}\tau(x)\big|\leq e^{-c_{k}|x|},\qquad\forall k\geq 0,\ x\in\mathbb{R}^{3}. $$

If $n$ is the same for all addends, then we say $u$ is admissible of degree $n$ . Otherwise, taking $n$ as the minimal one among all addends, we say $u$ is admissible of degree $\geq n$ .

Here are some properties of admissible functions.

#### Lemma 2.2.

Let $n,m\in\mathbb{N}$ and $u,v$ be admissible of degree $n,m$ , respectively. Then

- (1) $\forall j$ , $\frac{\partial u}{\partial\alpha_{j}}$ is admissible of degree $1+n$ , and $\frac{\partial u}{\partial\beta_{j}},\frac{\partial u}{\partial\lambda_{j}}$ are admissible of degree $n$ .

- (2) $uv$ is admissible of degree $n+m$ ;

- (3) $\phi_{u}v$ is admissible of degree $n+m$ ;

- (4) $\forall k\geq 1$ , $\psi_{u}^{(k)}v$ is admissible of degree $k+n+m$ ;

- (5) $\forall N\geq 1$ , $\phi_{u}^{(N)}v$ is admissible of degree $\geq 1+n+m$ ;

- (6) $\exists c>0$ such that for any compact set $K\subset\mathbb{R}^{3m}\times\mathbb{R}_{+}^{m}$ , $\exists C_{K}>0$ such that (2.22)

$$ |u(\alpha,\beta,\gamma,x)|\leq\frac{C_{K}}{a^{n}}e^{-c|x|},\quad\forall(\beta,\gamma)\in K, $$

where $a=\min\limits_{j\neq k}|\alpha_{j}-\alpha_{k}|$ as in (2.1).

The proof of these properties is direct so we shall omit it. The point of considering admissible functions is that according to (6), they decay rapidly when $n$ is large.

Consider the linearized operators $L_{+},L_{-}$ around $Q$ defined by

$$ L_{+}f:=-\Delta f+f+\phi_{Q^{2}}f+2\phi_{Qf}Q,\quad L_{-}f:=-\Delta f+f+\phi_{Q^{2}}f. $$

By Theorem 4 in [9], $\{\partial_{1}Q,\partial_{2}Q,\partial_{3}Q\}$ spans $\ker L_{+}$ , and $\{Q\}$ spans $\ker L_{-}$ . Moreover, Lemma 2.4 in [8] asserts that when restricted to admissible functions, $\ker(L_{\pm})^{\perp}$ is exactly the range of $L_{\pm}$ . A precise statement is as follows.

#### Lemma 2.3.

Let $n\in\mathbb{N}$ and $f$ be real-valued and admissible of degree $n$ .

- (1) If $(f,\nabla Q)=0$ , then $L_{+}u=f$ has a real-valued solution $u$ admissible of degree $n$ .

- (2) If $(f,Q)=0$ , then $L_{-}u=f$ has a real-valued solution $u$ admissible of degree $n$ .

Furthermore, if $f$ is radial, then $u$ can be chosen to be radial.

The following proposition constructs the approximate solutions.

#### Proposition 2.4.

For $n\geq 1$ and $1\leq j\leq m$ , there exist real-valued $m_{j}^{(n)},b_{j}^{(n)}\in S_{n}$ and $T_{j}^{(n)}$ that is admissible of degree $n$ such that: for any $N\geq 1$ , if setting

$$ \displaystyle V_{j}^{(N)}(P,y_{j})=Q(y_{j})+\sum_{n=1}^{N}T_{j}^{(n)}(P,y_{j}), \displaystyle M_{j}^{(N)}(P)=\sum_{n=1}^{N}m_{j}^{(n)}(P)\quad\text{and}\quad B_{j}^{(N)}(P)=\sum_{n=1}^{N}b_{j}^{(n)}(P), $$

then $\tilde{E}_{j}^{(N)}$ defined by (2.16) is admissible of degree $\geq N+1$ .

#### Proof.

We construct the functions by induction in $N$ .

For $N=1$ , we take $m_{j}^{(1)}=b_{j}^{(1)}=0$ . Suppose $T_{j}^{(1)}$ is admissible of degree $1$ and real-valued. By Lemma 2.2 and (1.4), we have

$$ \displaystyle\tilde{E}_{j}^{(1)} \displaystyle=\Delta V_{j}^{(1)}-V_{j}^{(1)}+i\lambda_{j}^{2}\sum_{k=1}^{m}\frac{\partial V_{j}^{(1)}}{\partial\alpha_{k}}\cdot 2\beta_{k}-\bigg(\phi_{|V_{j}^{(1)}|^{2}}+\sum_{k\neq j}\psi_{|V_{k}^{(1)}|^{2}}^{(1)}\bigg)V_{j}^{(1)} \displaystyle=\Delta T_{j}^{(1)}-T_{j}^{(1)}-\phi_{Q^{2}}T_{j}^{(1)}-2\phi_{QT_{j}^{(1)}}Q-\sum_{k\neq j}\psi_{Q^{2},k}^{(1)}Q+error \displaystyle=-L_{+}T_{j}^{(1)}+\sum_{k\neq j}\frac{\lambda_{j}^{2}\|Q\|_{L^{2}}^{2}}{4\pi\lambda_{k}|\alpha_{jk}|}Q+error, $$

where $error$ is admissible of degree $\geq 2$ . Since $L_{+}(\Lambda Q)=-2Q$ , we may take

$$ T_{j}^{(1)}=-\sum_{k\neq j}\frac{\lambda_{j}^{2}\|Q\|_{L^{2}}^{2}}{8\pi\lambda_{k}|\alpha_{jk}|}\Lambda Q $$

to cancel the first two terms. This proves the conclusion when $N=1$ .

Next, we construct $m_{j}^{(N+1)},b_{j}^{(N+1)}$ and $T_{j}^{(N+1)}$ from the first $N$ terms. We have

$$ \displaystyle\tilde{E}_{j}^{(N+1)}-\tilde{E}_{j}^{(N)} \displaystyle=\Delta T_{j}^{(N+1)}-T_{j}^{(N+1)}-i\lambda_{j}m_{j}^{(N+1)}\Lambda Q-\lambda_{j}^{3}b_{j}^{(N+1)}\cdot y_{j}Q \displaystyle-\phi_{Q^{2}}T_{j}^{(N+1)}-2\phi_{\mathrm{Re}\left(Q\overline{T_{j}^{(N+1)}}\right)}Q-\sum_{k\neq j}\psi_{Q^{2},k}^{(N+1)}Q+error \displaystyle=-\Big(L_{+}X_{j}^{(N+1)}+\lambda_{j}^{3}b_{j}^{(N+1)}\cdot y_{j}Q+\sum_{k\neq j}\psi_{Q^{2},k}^{(N+1)}Q\Big) \displaystyle-i\left(L_{-}Y_{j}^{(N+1)}+\lambda_{j}m_{j}^{(N+1)}\Lambda Q\right)+error, $$

where

$$ X_{j}^{(N+1)}=\mathrm{Re}\ T_{j}^{(N+1)},\quad Y_{j}^{(N+1)}=\mathrm{Im}\ T_{j}^{(N+1)},\quad error=I_{1}+I_{2}+I_{3}+I_{4}, $$

and

$$ \displaystyle I_{1} \displaystyle=-i\lambda_{j}m_{j}^{(N+1)}\Lambda\left(V_{j}^{(N+1)}-Q\right)-i\lambda_{j}M_{j}^{(N)}\Lambda T_{j}^{(N+1)} \displaystyle\quad-\lambda_{j}^{3}b_{j}^{(N+1)}\cdot y_{j}\left(V_{j}^{(N+1)}-Q\right)-\lambda_{j}^{3}B_{j}^{(N)}\cdot y_{j}T_{j}^{(N+1)}, $$

$$ \displaystyle I_{2} \displaystyle=-\phi_{\left|V_{j}^{(N)}\right|^{2}-Q^{2}}T_{j}^{(N+1)}-2\phi_{\mathrm{Re}\left(V_{j}^{(N)}\overline{T_{j}^{(N+1)}}\right)}\left(V_{j}^{(N+1)}-Q\right) \displaystyle\quad-2\phi_{\mathrm{Re}\left(\left(V_{j}^{(N)}-Q\right)\overline{T_{j}^{(N+1)}}\right)}Q-\phi_{\left|T_{j}^{(N+1)}\right|^{2}}V_{j}^{(N+1)}, $$

$$ \displaystyle I_{3} \displaystyle=-\sum_{k\neq j}\Bigg(\psi_{\left|V_{k}^{(N)}\right|^{2}-Q^{2}}^{(N+1)}V_{j}^{(N+1)}+\psi_{Q^{2},k}^{(N+1)}\left(V_{j}^{(N+1)}-Q\right)+\phi_{\left|V_{k}^{(N)}\right|^{2}}^{(N)}T_{j}^{(N+1)} \displaystyle\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad+2\phi_{\mathrm{Re}\left(V_{k}^{(N)}\overline{T_{k}^{(N+1)}}\right)}^{(N)}V_{j}^{(N+1)}+\phi_{\left|T_{k}^{(N+1)}\right|^{2}}^{(N)}V_{j}^{(N+1)}\Bigg), $$

$$ \displaystyle I_{4} \displaystyle=i\lambda_{j}^{2}\sum_{k=1}^{m}\Bigg(\frac{\partial T_{j}^{(N+1)}}{\partial\alpha_{k}}\cdot 2\beta_{k}+\frac{\partial T_{j}^{(N+1)}}{\partial\beta_{k}}\cdot B_{k}^{(N)}+\frac{\partial V_{j}^{(N+1)}}{\partial\beta_{k}}\cdot b_{k}^{(N+1)} \displaystyle\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\quad+\frac{\partial T_{j}^{(N+1)}}{\partial\lambda_{k}}\cdot M_{k}^{(N)}+\frac{\partial V_{j}^{(N+1)}}{\partial\lambda_{k}}\cdot m_{k}^{(N+1)}\Bigg). $$

Assume $m_{j}^{(N+1)},b_{j}^{(N+1)}\in S_{N+1}$ and $T_{j}^{(N+1)}$ is admissible of degree $N+1$ . Using Lemma 2.2, we see $error$ is admissible of degree $\geq N+2$ . Thus it suffices to require

$$ \left\{\begin{aligned} &L_{+}X_{j}^{(N+1)}=-\lambda_{j}^{3}b_{j}^{(N+1)}\cdot y_{j}Q-\sum_{k\neq j}\psi_{Q^{2},k}^{(N+1)}Q+\mathrm{Re}\ \hat{E}_{j}^{(N)},\\
&L_{-}Y_{j}^{(N+1)}=-\lambda_{j}m_{j}^{(N+1)}\Lambda Q+\mathrm{Im}\ \hat{E}_{j}^{(N)},\end{aligned}\right. $$

where $\hat{E}_{j}^{(N)}$ is the sum of terms in $\tilde{E}_{j}^{(N)}$ that are admissible of degree $N+1$ .

Recall that we let the right hand sides be functions of $y_{j}$ , so they are admissible of degree $N+1$ . By Lemma 2.3, it suffices to require

$$ \left\{\begin{aligned} &\Big(\lambda_{j}^{3}b_{j}^{(N+1)}\cdot y_{j}Q+\sum_{k\neq j}\psi_{Q^{2},k}^{(N+1)}Q-\mathrm{Re}\ \hat{E}_{j}^{(N)},\nabla Q\Big)=0,\\
&\left(\lambda_{j}m_{j}^{(N+1)}\Lambda Q-\mathrm{Im}\ \hat{E}_{j}^{(N)},Q\right)=0.\end{aligned}\right. $$

Such $b_{j}^{(N+1)}$ and $m_{j}^{(N+1)}$ exist because $(y_{j}Q,\nabla Q)\neq 0$ and $(\Lambda Q,Q)\neq 0$ . ∎

### 2.2. Accuracy of approximate solutions

We verify the accuracy of $R^{(N)}$ as an approximate solution where $V_{j}^{(N)}$ is determined in Proposition 2.4. We start with some estimates following from the definition of admissible functions.

Let $\tilde{\Omega}=\Omega\times(\mathbb{R}/2\pi\mathbb{Z})^{m}$ denote the space of modulation parameters and $g\in\tilde{\Omega}$ . If $K$ is a compact set in $\mathbb{R}^{3m}\times\mathbb{R}_{+}^{m}$ and $(\beta,\gamma)\in K$ , then by (1.6) and (2.22), we have

$$ |V_{j}^{(N)}|\leq Ce^{-c|y_{j}|}+C_{N}a^{-1}e^{-c_{N}|y_{j}|}, $$

which also yields

$$ |R_{j,g}^{(N)}|\leq Ce^{-c|x-\alpha_{j}|}+C_{N}a^{-1}e^{-c_{N}|x-\alpha_{j}|}. $$

By definition, $R_{g}^{(N)}$ is $C^{1}$ in $g$ . Thus, if $g^{\prime}\in\Omega$ and $(\beta^{\prime},\gamma^{\prime})\in K$ , then

$$ \left\|R^{(N)}_{g}-R^{(N)}_{g^{\prime}}\right\|_{H^{1}}\leq C_{N}\|g-g^{\prime}\|. $$

Finally, since $m_{j}^{(1)}=b_{j}^{(1)}=0$ , we have

$$ |M_{j}^{(N)}|\leq Ca^{-2}+C_{N}a^{-3},\quad|B_{j}^{(N)}|\leq Ca^{-2}+C_{N}a^{-3}. $$

Here, the capital constants depend on $K$ , while the little ones do not.

The next lemma consists of two localization properties. The first item shows that the cross term about $R_{j}$ in (2.13) does not matter. The second item will be used later.

#### Lemma 2.5.

Let $p\neq q\in\mathbb{R}^{3}$ and $u,v$ be functions such that

$$ |u(x)|\leq e^{-|x-p|},\quad|v(x)|\leq e^{-|x-q|},\quad\forall x\in\mathbb{R}^{3}. $$

Then there exist absolute constants $C,c>0$ such that:

- (1) $\|\phi_{uv}\|_{L^{\infty}}\leq Ce^{-c|p-q|}$ ;

- (2) If $f\in L^{2}$ , then $\|\phi_{fu}fv\|_{L^{1}}\leq C\max\Big\{\frac{e^{-\frac{1}{2}|p-q|}}{|p-q|^{\frac{1}{2}}},\frac{1}{|p-q|}\Big\}\|f\|_{L^{2}}^{2}$ .

#### Proof.

(1) Using the Hardy-Littlewood-Sobolev inequality, we get $\|\phi_{uv}\|_{L^{\infty}}\leq C\|uv\|_{L^{3/2}}$ . Note that either $|x-p|\geq\frac{1}{2}|p-q|$ or $|x-q|\geq\frac{1}{2}|p-q|$ . In the first case, we use $|u(x)|\leq e^{-c|p-q|}$ and $\|v\|_{L^{3/2}}\leq C$ to conclude, and the second case is similar.

(2) We have

$$ \|\phi_{fu}fv\|_{L^{1}}\leq C\iint\frac{|f(x)||f(y)|}{|x-y|}e^{-|x-p|-|y-q|}\mathrm{d}x\mathrm{d}y $$

The integral on the region $|x-y|\geq\frac{1}{2}|p-q|$ is easily bounded by $\frac{C}{|p-q|}\|f\|_{L^{2}}^{2}$ .

If $|x-y|<\frac{1}{2}|p-q|$ , then $|x-p|+|y-q|\geq\frac{1}{2}|p-q|+\frac{1}{4}|x-p|$ , so by Cauchy-Schwarz,

$$ \displaystyle\iint_{|x-y|<\frac{1}{2}|p-q|}\frac{|f(x)||f(y)|}{|x-y|}e^{-|x-p|-|y-q|}\mathrm{d}x\mathrm{d}y \displaystyle\leq \displaystyle e^{-\frac{1}{2}|p-q|}\int|f(x)|e^{-\frac{1}{4}|x-p|}\Big(\int_{|y-x|\leq\frac{1}{2}|p-q|}\frac{|f(y)|}{|y-x|}\mathrm{d}y\Big)\mathrm{d}x \displaystyle\leq \displaystyle Ce^{-\frac{1}{2}|p-q|}|p-q|^{-\frac{1}{2}}\|f\|_{L^{2}}\int|f(x)|e^{-\frac{1}{4}|x-p|}\mathrm{d}x\leq C\frac{e^{-\frac{1}{2}|p-q|}}{|p-q|^{\frac{1}{2}}}\|f\|_{L^{2}}^{2}. $$

We then obtain the conclusion. ∎

The following is the main result in this subsection. It estimates the extent to which $R_{g}^{(N)}$ , defined by (2.12), satisfies the Hartree equation (1.1).

#### Proposition 2.6.

Let $c_{0},C_{0}>0$ and suppose $g\in C^{1}(\mathbb{R}_{+},\tilde{\Omega})$ satisfies

$$ a\geq c_{0},\quad|\beta|\leq C_{0},\quad c_{0}\leq\lambda_{j}\leq C_{0}. $$

Let $V_{j}^{(N)}$ , $M_{j}^{(N)}$ and $B_{j}^{(N)}$ be as in Proposition 2.4, $R_{g}^{(N)}$ be defined by (2.12), and

$$ \Psi^{(N)}=i\partial_{t}R_{g}^{(N)}+\Delta R_{g}^{(N)}-\phi_{|R_{g}^{(N)}|^{2}}R_{g}^{(N)}-\sum_{j=1}^{m}\frac{1}{\lambda_{j}^{4}}S_{j}^{(N)}e^{-i\gamma_{j}+i\beta_{j}\cdot x}. $$

Then there exist $c,C>0$ depending on $c_{0}$ , $C_{0}$ and $N$ such that

$$ |\Psi^{(N)}(t,x)|\leq\frac{C}{a^{N+1}(t)}\max\limits_{j}e^{-c|x-\alpha_{j}(t)|}. $$

#### Proof.

For simplicity, we omit the superscript $N$ and the subscript $g$ .

By (2.13), we have

$$ \displaystyle\Psi \displaystyle=\sum_{j=1}^{m}\frac{1}{\lambda_{j}^{4}}\tilde{E}_{j}(t,y_{j})e^{-i\gamma_{j}+i\beta_{j}\cdot x}+\sum_{j\neq k}\phi_{\mathrm{Re}(R_{j}\overline{R_{k}})}R \displaystyle+\sum_{j=1}^{m}\frac{1}{\lambda_{j}^{4}}\sum_{k\neq j}\left[\phi_{\left|V_{k}\right|^{2}}^{(N)}-\left(\frac{\lambda_{j}}{\lambda_{k}}\right)^{2}\phi_{|V_{k}|^{2}}\left(P(t),\frac{\lambda_{j}}{\lambda_{k}}y_{j}+\frac{\alpha_{jk}}{\lambda_{k}}\right)\right]V_{j}e^{-i\gamma_{j}+i\beta_{j}\cdot x}. $$

The first term is controlled using Proposition 2.4 and (2.22). The second term is controlled using Lemma 2.5 and (2.39). For the last term, we claim that

$$ \left|\phi_{\left|V_{k}\right|^{2}}^{(N)}-\left(\frac{\lambda_{j}}{\lambda_{k}}\right)^{2}\phi_{|V_{k}|^{2}}\left(\frac{\lambda_{j}}{\lambda_{k}}y_{j}+\frac{\alpha_{jk}}{\lambda_{k}}\right)\right|\leq\left\{\begin{aligned} &C(1+|y_{j}|)^{N},\ \lambda_{j}|y_{j}|\geq\frac{|\alpha_{jk}|}{3},\\
&\frac{C(1+|y_{j}|)^{N}}{|\alpha_{jk}|^{N+1}},\ \lambda_{j}|y_{j}|\leq\frac{|\alpha_{jk}|}{3}.\end{aligned}\right. $$

Since $F_{n}$ is homogeneous of degree $n$ in $\zeta$ , using (2.38) and the Hardy-Littlewood-Sobolev inequality, we see the left hand side of (2.49) is always bounded by $C(1+|y_{j}|)^{N}$ , so we focus on the case when $\lambda_{j}|y_{j}|\leq\frac{|\alpha_{jk}|}{3}$ . We write

$$ \displaystyle LHS \displaystyle=\frac{\lambda_{j}^{2}}{4\pi\lambda_{k}}\int|V_{k}(\xi)|^{2}\Big|\frac{1}{|\alpha_{jk}-\lambda_{k}\xi+\lambda_{j}y_{j}|}-\sum_{n=1}^{N}F_{n}(\alpha_{jk},\lambda_{k}\xi-\lambda_{j}y_{j})\Big|\mathrm{d}\xi \displaystyle=\frac{\lambda_{j}^{2}}{4\pi\lambda_{k}}\left(\int_{\lambda_{k}|\xi|\geq\frac{|\alpha_{jk}|}{3}}+\int_{\lambda_{k}|\xi|\leq\frac{|\alpha_{jk}|}{3}}\right)\triangleq\frac{\lambda_{j}^{2}}{4\pi\lambda_{k}}(I_{1}+I_{2}). $$

By Hardy-Littlewood-Sobolev, the definition of $F_{n}$ and (2.38), we have

$$ \displaystyle I_{1} \displaystyle\leq C\left\|V_{k}(\xi)\chi_{\{\lambda_{k}|\xi|\geq\frac{|\alpha_{jk}|}{3}\}}\right\|_{L^{8/3}}^{2}+C\left\||V_{k}(\xi)|^{2}\big(1+|\xi|\big)^{N}\chi_{\{\lambda_{k}|\xi|\geq\frac{|\alpha_{jk}|}{3}\}}\right\|_{L^{1}} \displaystyle\leq Ce^{-c|\alpha_{jk}|}\leq\frac{C(1+|y_{j}|)^{N}}{|\alpha_{jk}|^{N+1}}. $$

By the Taylor formula,

$$ \Big|\frac{1}{|\alpha-\zeta|}-\sum_{n=1}^{N}F_{n}(\alpha,\zeta)\Big|\leq C\frac{|\zeta|^{N}}{|\alpha|^{N+1}},\quad\text{if }|\zeta|\leq\frac{|\alpha|}{3}, $$

so by the assumption that $\lambda_{j}|y_{j}|\leq\frac{|\alpha_{jk}|}{3}$ and (2.38), we have

$$ I_{2}\leq\frac{C(1+|y_{j}|)^{N}}{|\alpha_{jk}|^{N+1}}\int|V_{k}(\xi)|^{2}(1+|\xi|)^{N}\mathrm{d}\xi\leq\frac{C(1+|y_{j}|)^{N}}{|\alpha_{jk}|^{N+1}}. $$

Thus (2.49) holds. Note that this yields

$$ \left|\phi_{\left|V_{k}\right|^{2}}^{(N)}-\left(\frac{\lambda_{j}}{\lambda_{k}}\right)^{2}\phi_{|V_{k}|^{2}}\left(\frac{\lambda_{j}}{\lambda_{k}}y_{j}+\frac{\alpha_{jk}}{\lambda_{k}}\right)\right|\leq\frac{C(1+|y_{j}|)^{2N}}{a^{N+1}}. $$

Then by (2.38), we can control the first term. ∎

From the estimate (2.47), if $N$ is large, then the error $\Psi^{(N)}$ will decay rapidly in time. This helps us overcome the long range effect of (1.1). This is also why we need to construct the approximate solution. From now on, the strategy becomes also similar to that of [16].

## 3. Reduction of the problem

Now we will focus on the hyperbolic case. Note that we do not have any additional assumption on the masses. We may still state the result in a more general way, for instance writing $a(t)$ instead of $t$ , so that it is easier to apply it to the other two cases.

In this section, we perform two steps of reduction of the hyperbolic problem.

### 3.1. Uniform estimates

Due to (2.46), we want $S_{j}^{(N)}$ to vanish. Thus we need the following ODE result. It essentially states that the equation $S_{j}^{(N)}=0$ can be understood as a perturbation of the $m$ -body problem (1.8).

#### Proposition 3.1.

Let $P^{\infty}$ be a hyperbolic solution to (1.8) of the form (1.13), and $B_{j}^{(N)},M_{j}^{(N)}$ be as determined in Proposition 2.4. Then there exist $T_{0}=T_{0}(N)>0$ and $P^{(N)}\in C^{1}\big([T_{0},+\infty),\Omega\big)$ such that

$$ \left\{\begin{aligned} \dot{\alpha}_{j}^{(N)}(t)&=2\beta_{j}^{(N)}(t),\\
\dot{\beta}_{j}^{(N)}(t)&=B_{j}^{(N)}\left(P^{(N)}(t)\right),\\
\dot{\lambda}_{j}^{(N)}(t)&=M_{j}^{(N)}\left(P^{(N)}(t)\right),\end{aligned}\right.\qquad\forall t\geq T_{0} $$

and

$$ \left\|P^{(N)}(t)-P^{\infty}(t)\right\|\leq t^{-1/2},\qquad\forall t\geq T_{0}. $$

We need the exact expression of $b_{j}^{(2)}$ . Since $T_{j}^{(1)}$ is real-valued, we have

$$ \mathrm{Re}\ \hat{E}_{j}^{(1)}=-2\phi_{QT_{j}^{(1)}}T_{j}^{(1)}-\phi_{\left|T_{j}^{(1)}\right|^{2}}Q-\sum_{k\neq j}\left(2\psi_{QT_{k}^{(1)}}^{(1)}Q+\psi_{Q^{2},k}^{(1)}T_{k}^{(1)}\right). $$

Since $T_{j}^{(1)}$ is even, by the explicit formula of $\psi^{(1)}$ , $\mathrm{Re}\ \hat{E}_{j}^{(1)}$ is also even, and thus orthogonal to $\nabla Q$ . We then obtain by the proof of Proposition 2.4 that

$$ \Big(\lambda_{j}^{3}b_{j}^{(2)}\cdot y_{j}Q+\sum_{k\neq j}\psi_{Q^{2},k}^{(2)}Q,\nabla Q\Big)=0. $$

By the explicit formula of $\psi^{(2)}$ and using $Q$ is even, we deduce

$$ b_{j}^{(2)}(P)=-\sum_{k\neq j}\frac{\|Q\|_{L^{2}}^{2}\alpha_{jk}}{4\pi\lambda_{k}|\alpha_{jk}|^{3}}. $$

Note that this is exactly the gravitational force acting on the $j$ -th body. This explains the reason why we expect the $m$ -body interaction and our choice of the coefficients. Also, (3.1) can be viewed as a perturbation of the $m$ -body equation (1.8).

#### Proof of Proposition 3.1.

Let $\epsilon=\frac{1}{10}$ and $T_{0}>0$ . Define the norm $\|\cdot\|_{1}$ of $P\in C\big([T_{0},+\infty),\Omega\big)$ by

$$ \|P\|_{1}:=\sum_{j=1}^{m}\sup_{t\geq T_{0}}\Big(t^{1-3\epsilon}|\alpha_{j}(t)|+t^{2-2\epsilon}|\beta_{j}(t)|+t^{1-\epsilon}|\lambda_{j}(t)|\Big). $$

Let $X=\Big\{P\in C\big([T_{0},+\infty),\Omega\big)\ \big|\ \|P-P^{\infty}\|_{1}\leq 1\Big\}$ and define $\Gamma P(t)$ by

$$ \begin{gathered}\Gamma\alpha_{j}(t)=\alpha_{j}^{\infty}(t)+\int_{t}^{\infty}2(\beta_{j}^{\infty}(\tau)-\beta_{j}(\tau))\mathrm{d}\tau,\\
\Gamma\beta_{j}(t)=\lim_{t\to\infty}\beta_{j}^{\infty}(t)-\int_{t}^{\infty}B_{j}^{(N)}(P(\tau))\mathrm{d}\tau,\\
\Gamma\lambda_{j}(t)=\lambda_{j}^{\infty}-\int_{t}^{\infty}M_{j}^{(N)}(P(\tau))\mathrm{d}\tau.\end{gathered} $$

Because of the decay of $a$ in $t$ , we know $\lim\limits_{t\to\infty}\beta_{j}^{\infty}(t)$ does exist.

We claim that: if $T_{0}(N)$ is large enough, then $\Gamma$ maps $X$ into $X$ , and for $P,P^{\prime}\in X$ , we have $\|\Gamma P-\Gamma P^{\prime}\|_{1}\leq\frac{1}{2}\|P-P^{\prime}\|_{1}$ .

Assume $P\in X$ . Since $P^{\infty}$ is hyperbolic, we have $a(t)\gtrsim t$ . First,

$$ |\Gamma\alpha_{j}(t)-\alpha_{j}^{\infty}(t)|\leq 2\int_{t}^{\infty}|\beta_{j}(\tau)-\beta_{j}^{\infty}(\tau)|\mathrm{d}\tau\leq 2\int_{t}^{\infty}\tau^{2\epsilon-2}\mathrm{d}\tau\leq Ct^{2\epsilon-1}. $$

Using $b_{j}^{(1)}=0$ and $b_{j}^{(2)}(P^{\infty}(t))=\dot{\beta}_{j}^{\infty}(t)$ , which comes from (3.5), we have

$$ |\Gamma\beta_{j}(t)-\beta_{j}^{\infty}(t)|\leq\int_{t}^{\infty}\big|b_{j}^{(2)}(P(\tau))-b_{j}^{(2)}(P^{\infty}(\tau))\big|\mathrm{d}\tau+\sum_{n=3}^{N}\int_{t}^{\infty}\big|b_{j}^{(n)}(P(\tau))\big|\mathrm{d}\tau. $$

By the fundamental theorem of calculus, we have

$$ \big|b_{j}^{(2)}(P(\tau))-b_{j}^{(2)}(P^{\infty}(\tau))\big|\leq C\left(\frac{|\alpha-\alpha^{\infty}|}{a^{3}}+\frac{|\beta-\beta^{\infty}|}{a^{2}}+\frac{|\lambda-\lambda^{\infty}|}{a^{2}}\right)\leq C\tau^{\epsilon-3}, $$

and thus, using $b_{j}^{(n)}\in S_{n}$ , we get

$$ |\Gamma\beta_{j}(t)-\beta_{j}^{\infty}(t)|\leq C\int_{t}^{\infty}\tau^{\epsilon-3}\mathrm{d}\tau+C_{N}\sum_{n=3}^{N}\int_{t}^{\infty}\tau^{-n}\mathrm{d}\tau\leq C_{N}t^{\epsilon-2}. $$

Using $m_{j}^{(1)}=0$ and $m_{j}^{(n)}\in S_{n}$ , we have

$$ \displaystyle|\Gamma\lambda_{j}(t)-\lambda_{j}^{\infty}(t)|\leq\sum_{n=2}^{N}\int_{t}^{\infty}\big|m_{j}^{(n)}(P(\tau))\big|\mathrm{d}\tau\leq C_{N}\sum_{n=2}^{N}\int_{t}^{\infty}\tau^{-n}\mathrm{d}\tau\leq C_{N}t^{-1}. $$

Collecting the above estimates, we get $\|\Gamma P\|_{1}\leq C_{N}T_{0}^{-\epsilon}$ .

Thus for $T_{0}(N)$ large enough, we have $\Gamma:X\to X$ . The contraction property can be checked in the same way. By the contraction mapping theorem, $\Gamma$ has a unique fixed point in $X$ . Taking this fixed point as $P^{(N)}$ , then the requirements are satisfied. ∎

From Proposition 2.6 and 3.1, we know $R_{g^{(N)}}^{(N)}$ is almost a solution of (1.1). We then reduce the hyperbolic case to the following uniform estimate with a bootstrap assumption.

#### Proposition 3.2.

Let $P^{(N)}$ be defined as in Proposition 3.1 and $\gamma_{j}^{(N)}(t)$ be such that

$$ \gamma_{j}^{(N)}(0)=0,\quad\dot{\gamma}_{j}^{(N)}(t)=-\frac{1}{\lambda_{j}^{(N)}(t)^{2}}+|\beta_{j}^{(N)}(t)|^{2}+\dot{\beta}_{j}^{(N)}(t)\cdot\alpha_{j}^{(N)}(t). $$

Let $T_{n}\to+\infty$ and $u_{n}$ be the solution to

$$ \left\{\begin{aligned} &i\partial_{t}u_{n}+\Delta u_{n}-\phi_{|u_{n}|^{2}}u_{n}=0,\\
&u_{n}(T_{n},\cdot)=R_{g^{(N)}}^{(N)}(T_{n},\cdot).\end{aligned}\right. $$

Then there exists $T_{0}=T_{0}(N)$ such that for $N$ large and $T_{*}\in[T_{0},T_{n}]$ , if

$$ \left\|u_{n}(t)-R_{g^{(N)}}^{(N)}(t)\right\|_{H^{1}}\leq 2t^{-\frac{N}{9}},\qquad\forall n\geq 1,\ \forall t\in[T_{*},T_{n}], $$

then

$$ \left\|u_{n}(t)-R_{g^{(N)}}^{(N)}(t)\right\|_{H^{1}}\leq t^{-\frac{N}{9}},\qquad\forall n\geq 1,\ \forall t\in[T_{*},T_{n}]. $$

#### Proof of the hyperbolic case by Proposition 3.2.

Fix a large $N$ such that the conclusion holds. By the standard bootstrap argument, we know (3.15) actually holds with $T_{*}=T_{0}$ . Using (2.39), we know there exists $C>0$ such that

$$ \|u_{n}(t)\|_{H^{1}}\leq C,\quad\forall n\geq 1,\ \forall t\in[T_{0},T_{n}]. $$

Also, for any $\delta>0$ , there exist $r=r(\delta)>0$ and $t_{0}=t_{0}(\delta)>T_{0}$ such that

$$ \int_{|x|>r}|u_{n}(t_{0},x)|^{2}\mathrm{d}x<\delta,\quad\forall n\geq 1. $$

We claim that there exists $r^{\prime}=r^{\prime}(\delta)>0$ such that

$$ \int_{|x|>r^{\prime}}|u_{n}(T_{0},x)|^{2}\mathrm{d}x<2\delta,\quad\forall n\geq 1. $$

To prove (3.19), let $\Phi\in C^{\infty}(\mathbb{R})$ be a cutoff such that

$$ 0\leq\Phi\leq 1,\quad 0\leq\Phi^{\prime}\leq 2,\quad\Phi(x)=\left\{\begin{aligned} 0,&&x\leq 0,\\
1,&&x\geq 1.\end{aligned}\right. $$

Let $L>0$ and define $z(t)=\int|u_{n}(t,x)|^{2}\Phi(\frac{|x|-r}{L})\mathrm{d}x$ . Then $z(t_{0})\leq\delta$ . Since

$$ z^{\prime}(t)=-2\mathrm{Im}\int\Delta u_{n}\overline{u_{n}}\Phi\Big(\frac{|x|-r}{L}\Big)\mathrm{d}x=\frac{2}{L}\mathrm{Im}\int\nabla u_{n}\overline{u_{n}}\cdot\frac{x}{|x|}\Phi^{\prime}\Big(\frac{|x|-r}{L}\Big)\mathrm{d}x, $$

we have $|z^{\prime}(t)|\leq\frac{4}{L}\|u_{n}\|_{H^{1}}^{2}$ . Integrating in $t$ and using (3.17), we get

$$ \int_{|x|>L+r}|u_{n}(T_{0},x)|^{2}\mathrm{d}x\leq z(T_{0})\leq\frac{4C^{2}(t_{0}-T_{0})}{L}+\delta. $$

We deduce (3.19) by taking $L=L(\delta)$ large enough and $r^{\prime}=L+r$ .

Now, (3.17) and (3.19) imply the existence of a subsequence $u_{n_{k}}(T_{0})$ of $u_{n}(T_{0})$ that converges in $L^{2}$ to some $U_{0}$ and $U_{0}\in H^{1}$ . Let $U$ be the solution to

$$ \left\{\begin{aligned} &i\partial_{t}U+\Delta U-\phi_{|U|^{2}}U=0,\\
&U(T_{0})=U_{0}.\end{aligned}\right. $$

By global well-posedness of the equation, we have $u_{n_{k}}(t)\to U(t)$ in $L^{2}$ for any $t\geq T_{0}$ . Thanks to (3.17), by passing to subsequence, we may assume $u_{n_{k}}(t)\rightharpoonup U(t)$ in $H^{1}$ . Using (3.15) and Fatou’s lemma, we deduce

$$ \left\|U(t)-R_{g^{(N)}}^{(N)}(t)\right\|_{H^{1}}\leq 2t^{-\frac{N}{9}},\quad\forall t\geq T_{0}. $$

Let $\gamma^{\infty}(t)$ be such that

$$ \gamma_{j}^{\infty}(0)=0,\quad\dot{\gamma}_{j}^{\infty}(t)=-\frac{1}{(\lambda_{j}^{\infty})^{2}}+|\beta_{j}^{\infty}(t)|^{2}+\dot{\beta}_{j}^{\infty}(t)\cdot\alpha_{j}^{\infty}(t). $$

Then by (2.40), (3.2) and (2.22), we obtain the conclusion of the hyperbolic case. ∎

### 3.2. Modulation estimates

We want to find a family of modulation parameters $\alpha,\beta,\lambda$ and $\gamma$ such that $R_{g}^{(N)}$ is an orthogonal projection of $u_{n}$ . More precisely, we prove the following lemma.

#### Lemma 3.3.

Let $N,n\geq 1$ . Then there exist $T_{0}=T_{0}(N)>0$ and a unique modulation parameter $g\in C^{1}([T_{0},+\infty),\tilde{\Omega})$ such that: if

$$ \varepsilon(t,x)=u_{n}(t,x)-R_{g}^{(N)}(t,x), $$

then for $t\geq T_{0}$ and $1\leq j\leq m$ , we have

$$ \displaystyle\mathrm{Re}\Big(\varepsilon(t),g_{j}V_{j}^{(N)}\Big)=\mathrm{Re}\Big(\varepsilon(t),g_{j}\big(y_{j}V_{j}^{(N)}\big)\Big) \displaystyle= \displaystyle\mathrm{Im}\Big(\varepsilon(t),g_{j}\big(\Lambda V_{j}^{(N)}\big)\Big)=\mathrm{Im}\Big(\varepsilon(t),g_{j}\big(\nabla V_{j}^{(N)}\big)\Big)=0. $$

In particular, we have

$$ g(T_{n})=g^{(N)}(T_{n}),\quad\varepsilon(T_{n})=0. $$

To prove the above result, we first work on a time-independent version.

#### Lemma 3.4.

Let $N\geq 1$ and $K\subset\mathbb{R}_{+}^{m}$ be compact. Then there exist $\delta,A>0$ such that: if $g^{0}\in\tilde{\Omega}$ and $u\in H^{1}$ satisfy $a^{0}>A$ , $\lambda^{0}\in K$ and $\big\|u-R_{g^{0}}^{(N)}\big\|_{H^{1}}<\delta$ , then there exists a unique parameter $g\in\tilde{\Omega}$ that $C^{1}$ -depends on $u$ and

$$ \displaystyle\mathrm{Re}\Big(u-R_{g}^{(N)},g_{j}V_{j}^{(N)}\Big)=\mathrm{Re}\Big(u-R_{g}^{(N)},g_{j}\big(y_{j}V_{j}^{(N)}\big)\Big) \displaystyle= \displaystyle\mathrm{Im}\Big(u-R_{g}^{(N)},g_{j}\big(\Lambda V_{j}^{(N)}\big)\Big)=\mathrm{Im}\Big(u-R_{g}^{(N)},g_{j}\big(\nabla V_{j}^{(N)}\big)\Big)=0. $$

#### Proof.

Let $p=(g,u)$ and $\varepsilon(p)=u-R_{g}^{(N)}$ . Set $u_{0}=R_{g^{0}}^{(N)}$ and $p_{0}=(g_{0},u_{0})$ . Define

$$ \begin{gathered}\rho_{j}^{1}(p)=\mathrm{Re}\Big(\varepsilon(p),g_{j}V_{j}^{(N)}\Big),\quad\rho_{j}^{2}(p)=\mathrm{Re}\Big(\varepsilon(p),g_{j}\big(y_{j}V_{j}^{(N)}\big)\Big),\\
\rho_{j}^{3}(p)=\mathrm{Im}\Big(\varepsilon(p),g_{j}\big(\Lambda V_{j}^{(N)}\big)\Big),\quad\rho_{j}^{4}(p)=\mathrm{Im}\Big(\varepsilon(p),g_{j}\big(\nabla V_{j}^{(N)}\big)\Big).\end{gathered} $$

Then $\varepsilon(p_{0})=0$ and $\rho_{j}^{\nu}(p_{0})=0$ for $\nu=1,2,3,4$ .

We would like to compute $\frac{\partial\rho_{j}^{\nu}}{\partial g}(p_{0})$ . Since $\varepsilon(p_{0})=0$ , the partial derivative of $\rho_{j}^{\nu}$ evaluated at $p_{0}$ only falls on $\varepsilon$ . We compute

$$ \displaystyle\frac{\partial\varepsilon}{\partial\alpha_{j}} \displaystyle=-\frac{1}{\lambda_{j}}g_{j}\big(\nabla V_{j}^{(N)}\big)+g_{j}\Big(\frac{\partial V_{j}^{(N)}}{\partial\alpha_{j}}\Big), \displaystyle\frac{\partial\varepsilon}{\partial\beta_{j}} \displaystyle=i\alpha_{j}g_{j}V_{j}^{(N)}+i\lambda_{j}g_{j}\big(y_{j}V_{j}^{(N)}\big)+g_{j}\Big(\frac{\partial V_{j}^{(N)}}{\partial\beta_{j}}\Big), \displaystyle\frac{\partial\varepsilon}{\partial\lambda_{j}} \displaystyle=g_{j}\big(\Lambda V_{j}^{(N)}\big)+g_{j}\Big(\frac{\partial V_{j}^{(N)}}{\partial\lambda_{j}}\Big), \displaystyle\frac{\partial\varepsilon}{\partial\gamma_{j}} \displaystyle=-ig_{j}V_{j}^{(N)}. $$

Using (2.22), (2.38) and that $Q$ is real and even, we can represent $\frac{\partial\rho_{j}^{\nu}}{\partial g}(p_{0})$ by

|  | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| $\alpha$ | 0 | 1 | 0 | 0 |
| $\beta$ | 0 | 0 | * | 1 |
| $\lambda$ | 1 | 0 | 0 | 0 |
| $\gamma$ | 0 | 0 | 1 | 0 |

where $0$ , for instance the $(\alpha,1)$ entry, represents

$$ \frac{\partial\rho_{j}^{1}}{\partial\alpha_{k}}(p_{0})=o(1),\quad\forall j,k, $$

while $1$ , for instance the $(\alpha,2)$ entry, represents

$$ \frac{\partial\rho_{j}^{2}}{\partial\alpha_{k}}(p_{0})=\left\{\begin{matrix}o(1),&j\neq k,\\
c_{j}+o(1),&j=k.\end{matrix}\right. $$

Here $c_{j}$ is invertible and independent of $a$ , and $o(1)$ means goes to $0$ as $a\to+\infty$ .

Therefore, for $A$ large enough, $\frac{\partial\rho_{j}^{\nu}}{\partial g}(p_{0})$ is an invertible matrix. Then we can conclude by the implicit function theorem. The last comment is that $g\in\tilde{\Omega}$ because $g$ is closed to $g^{(N)}$ , which means we have $a>\frac{A}{2}$ when $\delta$ is small. ∎

#### Proof of Lemma 3.3.

By (3.15), for $T_{0}(N)$ large enough and $\delta,A$ determined in Lemma 3.4, if $t\geq T_{0}$ , then $a^{(N)}(t)>A$ and $\big\|u_{n}(t)-R_{g^{(N)}}^{(N)}(t)\big\|_{H^{1}}<\delta$ . By Lemma 3.4, there exists a unique $g(t)\in\tilde{\Omega}$ such that (3.27) holds. Moreover, $g\in C^{1}$ because $g$ is $C^{1}$ in $u_{n}$ and $u_{n}$ is $C^{1}$ in $t$ . ∎

It follows from the implicit function theorem that $g$ is closed to $g^{(N)}$ . But to prove Proposition 3.2, we need a quantitative estimate of $g-g^{(N)}$ and $\varepsilon$ .

#### Proposition 3.5.

For $N$ and $T_{0}=T_{0}(N)$ large enough, $\forall n\geq 1,\ T_{*}\in[T_{0},T_{n}]$ , if

$$ \left\{\begin{aligned} &\|\varepsilon(t)\|_{H^{1}}\leq t^{-\frac{N}{4}},\\
&\sum_{j=1}^{m}\left|\lambda_{j}(t)-\lambda_{j}^{(N)}(t)\right|+\left|\beta_{j}(t)-\beta_{j}^{(N)}(t)\right|\leq t^{-1-\frac{N}{8}},\\
&\sum_{j=1}^{m}\left|\gamma_{j}(t)-\gamma_{j}^{(N)}(t)\right|+\left|\alpha_{j}(t)-\alpha_{j}^{(N)}(t)\right|\leq t^{-\frac{N}{8}},\end{aligned}\right.\qquad\forall t\in[T_{*},T_{n}], $$

then

$$ \left\{\begin{aligned} &\|\varepsilon(t)\|_{H^{1}}\leq\frac{1}{2}t^{-\frac{N}{4}},\\
&\sum_{j=1}^{m}\left|\lambda_{j}(t)-\lambda_{j}^{(N)}(t)\right|+\left|\beta_{j}(t)-\beta_{j}^{(N)}(t)\right|\leq\frac{1}{2}t^{-1-\frac{N}{8}},\\
&\sum_{j=1}^{m}\left|\gamma_{j}(t)-\gamma_{j}^{(N)}(t)\right|+\left|\alpha_{j}(t)-\alpha_{j}^{(N)}(t)\right|\leq\frac{1}{2}t^{-\frac{N}{8}},\end{aligned}\right.\qquad\forall t\in[T_{*},T_{n}]. $$

#### Proof of Proposition 3.2 by Proposition 3.5.

As the left hand sides are continuous in $t$ , by a bootstrap argument, we know (3.34) actually holds for any $t\in[T_{0},T_{n}]$ . Then by (2.40), we have

$$ \displaystyle\left\|u_{n}(t)-R_{g^{(N)}}^{(N)}\right\|_{H^{1}} \displaystyle\leq\left\|u_{n}(t)-R_{g}^{(N)}\right\|_{H^{1}}+\left\|R_{g}^{(N)}-R_{g^{(N)}}^{(N)}\right\|_{H^{1}} \displaystyle\leq\|\varepsilon(t)\|_{H^{1}}+C_{N}\|g-g^{(N)}\|\leq t^{-\frac{N}{4}}+C_{N}t^{-\frac{N}{8}}\leq t^{-\frac{N}{9}} $$

when $T_{0}(N)$ is large enough. This finishes the proof of Proposition 3.2. ∎

So far, we have reduced the hyperbolic case to Proposition 3.5.

## 4. Estimates of the modulation

To simplify notations, we write $R_{j}=R_{j,g}^{(N)}$ , $R=R_{g}^{(N)}$ , $M_{j}=M_{j}^{(N)}$ , $B_{j}=B_{j}^{(N)}$ , $V_{j}=V_{j}^{(N)}$ , $S_{j}=S_{j}^{(N)}$ and $\Psi=\Psi^{(N)}$ . But we will make clear whether a constant depends on $N$ .

By (3.14) and (2.46), we have

$$ i\partial_{t}\varepsilon+\Delta\varepsilon-2\phi_{\mathrm{Re}(\varepsilon\overline{R})}R-\phi_{|R|^{2}}\varepsilon=\mathcal{N}(\varepsilon)-\Psi-\sum_{j=1}^{m}\frac{1}{\lambda_{j}^{4}}S_{j}(t,x)e^{-i\gamma_{j}+i\beta_{j}\cdot x}, $$

where

$$ \mathcal{N}(\varepsilon)=2\phi_{\mathrm{Re}(\varepsilon\overline{R})}\varepsilon+\phi_{|\varepsilon|^{2}}R+\phi_{|\varepsilon|^{2}}\varepsilon. $$

By the Sobolev inequality and the Hardy-Littlewood-Sobolev inequality, we have

$$ \|\mathcal{N}(\varepsilon)\|_{L^{2}}\leq C_{N}\|\varepsilon\|_{H^{1}}^{2}. $$

By (1.13), (3.2), (3.34) and (2.41), we have the following asymptotic properties:

$$ a(t)\sim t,\quad|\alpha_{j}|\lesssim t,\quad|\beta_{j}|\lesssim 1,\quad|\dot{\beta}_{j}|\lesssim\frac{1}{t^{2}},\quad\lambda_{j}\sim 1,\quad|\dot{\lambda}_{j}|\lesssim\frac{1}{t^{2}}. $$

In particular, (2.45) is satisfied.

### 4.1. Control of the parameters

In this subsection, we aim at proving the second and the third line of (3.35).

Define the modulation error

$$ \displaystyle Mod(t)=\sum_{j=1}^{m}\Bigg( \displaystyle\Big|\dot{\alpha}_{j}(t)-2\beta_{j}(t)\Big|+\Big|\dot{\beta}_{j}(t)-B_{j}(P(t))\Big|+\Big|\dot{\lambda}_{j}(t)-M_{j}(P(t))\Big| \displaystyle+\bigg|\dot{\gamma}_{j}(t)+\frac{1}{\lambda_{j}^{2}(t)}-|\beta_{j}(t)|^{2}-\dot{\beta}_{j}(t)\cdot\alpha_{j}(t)\bigg|\Bigg). $$

First notice that $S_{j}$ is controlled by $Mod$ :

$$ |S_{j}(t,x)|\leq C_{N}Mod(t)e^{-c_{N}|x-\alpha_{j}(t)|}. $$

Let $\theta(t,x)$ be a function such that

$$ |\theta(t,x)|\leq Ce^{-c|x|}+C_{N}a^{-1}e^{-c_{N}|x|},\quad\forall t>0,\ x\in\mathbb{R}^{3}, $$

which corresponds to (2.38), (2.39), and let $\theta_{j}=g_{j}\theta$ .

Using (4.1) and integration by parts, we can compute

$$ \displaystyle\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\mathrm{Im}\int\varepsilon\overline{\theta_{j}}= \displaystyle\mathrm{Re}\int\varepsilon\left(\overline{i\partial_{t}\theta_{j}+\Delta\theta_{j}-2\phi_{\mathrm{Re}(\theta_{j}\overline{R})}R-\phi_{|R|^{2}}\theta_{j}}\right) \displaystyle+\mathrm{Re}\int(\Psi-\mathcal{N}(\varepsilon))\overline{\theta_{j}}+\sum_{j=1}^{m}\mathrm{Re}\int\frac{1}{\lambda_{j}^{4}}S_{j}(t,x)e^{-i\gamma_{j}+i\beta_{j}\cdot x}\overline{\theta_{j}}. $$

By (2.4), (2.41) and (4.7), we have

$$ \displaystyle i\partial_{t}\theta_{j}+\Delta\theta_{j} \displaystyle=\frac{1}{\lambda_{j}^{4}}\left(i\lambda_{j}^{2}\partial_{t}\theta+\Delta\theta-\theta\right)e^{-i\gamma_{j}+i\beta_{j}\cdot x} \displaystyle+O\left(\frac{1}{a^{2}}+\frac{C_{N}}{a^{3}}+Mod\right)\left(e^{-c|x-\alpha_{j}|}+\frac{C_{N}}{a}e^{-c_{N}|x-\alpha_{j}|}\right). $$

By Lemma 2.5, (2.39) and (4.7), we have

$$ \displaystyle\phi_{\mathrm{Re}(\theta_{j}\overline{R})}R \displaystyle=\frac{1}{\lambda_{j}^{4}}\phi_{\mathrm{Re}(\theta\overline{V_{j}})}V_{j}e^{-i\gamma_{j}+i\beta_{j}\cdot x}+\phi_{\mathrm{Re}(\theta_{j}\overline{R}_{j})}\sum_{k\neq j}R_{k} \displaystyle+O_{N}\Big(e^{-c_{N}a}\max_{k}e^{-c_{N}|x-\alpha_{k}|}\Big). $$

By Lemma 2.5, (2.39), (4.7), (2.54) and the explicit formula of $\psi^{(2)}$ , we have

$$ \displaystyle\phi_{|R|^{2}}\theta_{j} \displaystyle=\frac{1}{\lambda_{j}^{4}}\bigg(\phi_{|V_{j}|^{2}}+\sum_{k\neq j}\psi_{|V_{k}|^{2}}^{(1)}\bigg)\theta e^{-i\gamma_{j}+i\beta_{j}\cdot x}+O\left(\frac{1}{a^{2}}e^{-c|x-\alpha_{j}|}\right) \displaystyle+O_{N}\Big((e^{-c_{N}a}+a^{-3})e^{-c_{N}|x-\alpha_{j}|}\Big). $$

We collect the terms of degree $1$ in $\theta$

$$ L_{j}\theta:=-\Delta\theta+\theta+2\phi_{\mathrm{Re}(\theta\overline{V_{j}})}V_{j}+\bigg(\phi_{|V_{j}|^{2}}+\sum_{k\neq j}\psi_{|V_{k}|^{2}}^{(1)}\bigg)\theta. $$

With (4.4), if we take $T_{0}(N)$ large enough, then we have

$$ \displaystyle i\partial_{t}\theta_{j}+\Delta\theta_{j}-2\phi_{\mathrm{Re}(\theta_{j}\overline{R})}R-\phi_{|R|^{2}}\theta_{j} \displaystyle= \displaystyle\frac{1}{\lambda_{j}^{4}}\left(i\lambda_{j}^{2}\partial_{t}\theta-L_{j}\theta\right)e^{-i\gamma_{j}+i\beta_{j}\cdot x}-2\phi_{\mathrm{Re}(\theta_{j}\overline{R}_{j})}\sum_{k\neq j}R_{k} \displaystyle+O\left(\frac{1}{a^{2}}+Mod\right)e^{-c|x-\alpha_{j}|}+O_{N}\left(\frac{1}{a^{3}}+\frac{Mod}{a}\right)e^{-c_{N}\min_{j}|x-\alpha_{j}|}. $$

Inserting this into the previous formula, using (2.47), (4.7), (4.3), and again taking $T_{0}(N)$ large enough, we get

$$ \displaystyle\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\mathrm{Im}\int\varepsilon\overline{\theta_{j}}= \displaystyle\mathrm{Re}\int\frac{\varepsilon}{\lambda_{j}^{4}}\overline{\left(i\lambda_{j}^{2}\partial_{t}\theta-L_{j}\theta\right)e^{-i\gamma_{j}+i\beta_{j}\cdot x}}-2\mathrm{Re}\int\varepsilon\phi_{\mathrm{Re}(\theta_{j}\overline{R}_{j})}\sum_{k\neq j}\overline{R_{k}} \displaystyle+\frac{1}{\lambda_{j}^{6}}\mathrm{Re}\int S_{j}\overline{\theta}+O\left(\frac{\|\varepsilon\|_{H^{1}}}{a^{2}}+Mod\|\varepsilon\|_{H^{1}}\right)+O_{N}\left(\frac{1}{a^{N+1}}+\|\varepsilon\|_{H^{1}}^{2}\right). $$

We will take $\theta$ to be $iV_{j}$ , $\nabla V_{j}$ , $\Lambda V_{j}$ and $iy_{j}V_{j}$ . By (3.27), the left hand side always vanishes. By (2.38), (4.4) and (2.41), we always have

$$ \partial_{t}\theta=O\left(\frac{1}{a^{2}}+\frac{C_{N}}{a^{3}}+\frac{Mod}{a}\right)\left(e^{-c|x-\alpha_{j}|}+\frac{C_{N}}{a}e^{-c_{N}|x-\alpha_{j}|}\right). $$

By the proof of Proposition 2.4, we know

$$ W_{j}:=-\Delta V_{j}+V_{j}+\bigg(\phi_{|V_{j}|^{2}}+\sum_{k\neq j}\psi_{|V_{k}|^{2}}^{(1)}\bigg)V_{j} $$

is admissible of degree $\geq 2$ . Direct computation yields

$$ \begin{gathered}L_{j}(iV_{j})=iW_{j},\quad L_{j}(\Lambda V_{j})=(\Lambda+2)W_{j}-2\bigg(1+\sum_{k\neq j}\psi_{|V_{k}|^{2}}^{(1)}\bigg)V_{j},\\
L_{j}(\nabla V_{j})=\nabla W_{j},\quad L_{j}(iy_{j}V_{j})=iy_{j}W_{j}-2i\nabla V_{j}.\end{gathered} $$

By (2.22), (3.27) and that $\psi^{(1)}$ is constant, we always have

$$ L_{j}\theta=f+O\left(\frac{1}{a^{2}}+\frac{C_{N}}{a^{3}}\right)\left(e^{-c|x-\alpha_{j}|}+\frac{C_{N}}{a}e^{-c_{N}|x-\alpha_{j}|}\right), $$

where $f$ is a function such that $\mathrm{Re}\int\varepsilon(\overline{g_{j}f})=0$ . Thus

$$ \mathrm{Re}\int\frac{\varepsilon}{\lambda_{j}^{4}}\overline{L_{j}\theta\ e^{-i\gamma_{j}+i\beta_{j}\cdot x}}=O\left(\frac{\|\varepsilon\|_{H^{1}}}{a^{2}}+\frac{C_{N}\|\varepsilon\|_{H^{1}}}{a^{3}}\right). $$

By (2.54) and the explicit formula of $\psi^{(2)}$ , we have

$$ \phi_{\mathrm{Re}(\theta_{j}\overline{R_{j}})}=\psi_{\mathrm{Re}(\theta_{j}\overline{R_{j}})}^{(1)}+O\left(\frac{1}{a^{2}}+\frac{C_{N}}{a^{3}}\right)\big(1+|x-\alpha_{j}|\big)^{2}. $$

Since $\psi^{(1)}$ is constant, by (3.27), we always have

$$ 2\mathrm{Re}\int\varepsilon\phi_{\mathrm{Re}(\theta_{j}\overline{R}_{j})}\sum_{k\neq j}\overline{R_{k}}=O\left(\frac{\|\varepsilon\|_{H^{1}}}{a^{2}}+\frac{C_{N}\|\varepsilon\|_{H^{1}}}{a^{3}}\right). $$

Finally, using (2.17), (2.38) and that $Q$ is even, for $\theta$ taken as the four functions,

$$ \sum_{\theta}\sum_{j=1}^{m}\left|\mathrm{Re}\int S_{j}\overline{\theta}\right|\geq c\ Mod-\frac{C_{N}Mod}{a}. $$

Therefore, gathering (4.15), (4.19), (4.21) and (4.22), we obtain

$$ Mod(t)\leq\frac{C\|\varepsilon\|_{H^{1}}}{a^{2}}+\frac{C_{N}\|\varepsilon\|_{H^{1}}}{a^{3}}+\frac{C_{N}Mod(t)}{a}+\frac{C_{N}}{a^{N+1}}+C_{N}\|\varepsilon\|_{H^{1}}^{2}. $$

Taking $T_{0}(N)$ large enough to absorb some $O_{N}$ terms, we get

$$ Mod(t)\leq\frac{C\|\varepsilon\|_{H^{1}}}{a^{2}}+\frac{C_{N}}{a^{N+1}}+C_{N}\|\varepsilon\|_{H^{1}}^{2}. $$

Using (3.34) and (4.4), we can get the decay of $Mod$ :

$$ Mod(t)\leq t^{-\frac{N}{4}},\qquad\forall t\in[T_{*},T_{n}]. $$

We are now going to deduce the second and third lines of (3.35). By the fundamental theorem of calculus, we have

$$ \displaystyle\big|M_{j}(P)-M_{j}(P^{(N)})\big|+\big|B_{j}(P)-B_{j}(P^{(N)})\big| \displaystyle\leq \displaystyle C\left(\frac{|\alpha-\alpha^{(N)}|}{a^{3}}+\frac{|\beta-\beta^{(N)}|}{a^{2}}+\frac{|\lambda-\lambda^{(N)}|}{a^{2}}\right) \displaystyle+C_{N}\left(\frac{|\alpha-\alpha^{(N)}|}{a^{4}}+\frac{|\beta-\beta^{(N)}|}{a^{3}}+\frac{|\lambda-\lambda^{(N)}|}{a^{3}}\right). $$

Using (3.1), (3.34), (4.4) and (4.25), if $T_{0}(N)$ is large enough, then we get

$$ \displaystyle\big|\dot{\lambda}_{j}-\dot{\lambda}_{j}^{(N)}\big|+\big|\dot{\beta}_{j}-\dot{\beta}_{j}^{(N)}\big| \displaystyle\leq \displaystyle Mod+\big|M_{j}(P)-M_{j}(P^{(N)})\big|+\big|B_{j}(P)-B_{j}(P^{(N)})\big|\leq Ct^{-2-\frac{N}{8}}. $$

Integrating in $t$ and using (3.28), we deduce

$$ \big|\lambda_{j}-\lambda_{j}^{(N)}\big|+\big|\beta_{j}-\beta_{j}^{(N)}\big|\leq\frac{C}{N}t^{-1-\frac{N}{8}}\leq\frac{1}{2}t^{-1-\frac{N}{8}} $$

when $N$ is large enough. This is the second line of (3.35).

By (4.25) and (4.4), we also have

$$ \big|\dot{\alpha}_{j}-\dot{\alpha}_{j}^{(N)}\big|\leq 2\big|\beta_{j}-\beta_{j}^{(N)}\big|+t^{-\frac{N}{4}} $$

and

$$ \big|\dot{\gamma}_{j}-\dot{\gamma}_{j}^{(N)}\big|\leq C\left(\big|\lambda_{j}-\lambda_{j}^{(N)}\big|+\big|\beta_{j}-\beta_{j}^{(N)}\big|+t\big|\dot{\beta}_{j}-\dot{\beta}_{j}^{(N)}\big|+\big|\dot{\alpha}_{j}-\dot{\alpha}_{j}^{(N)}\big|\right)+t^{-\frac{N}{4}}. $$

We then deduce the third line of (3.35) for large $N$ by (3.28) and (4.28).

### 4.2. Control of the error

In this subsection, we aim at proving the first line of (3.35). We start with the construction of cutoff functions.

#### Lemma 4.1.

There exist $c,C>0$ and $\varphi_{j}\in C^{1,\infty}(\mathbb{R}_{+}\times\mathbb{R}^{3})$ for $1\leq j\leq m$ such that

$$ \begin{gathered}0\leq\varphi_{j}(t,x)\leq 1,\quad\sum_{j=1}^{m}\varphi_{j}(t,x)\equiv 1,\\
|\partial_{t}\varphi_{j}|+|\nabla\varphi_{j}|\leq\frac{C}{a},\quad|\partial_{t}\sqrt{\varphi_{j}}|+|\nabla\sqrt{\varphi_{j}}|\leq\frac{C}{a},\\
\varphi_{j}(t,x)=\left\{\begin{aligned} &1,\quad|x-\alpha_{j}(t)|\leq ca(t),\\
&0,\quad|x-\alpha_{k}(t)|\leq ca(t),\ k\neq j.\end{aligned}\right.\end{gathered} $$

#### Proof.

There exist $c_{0},C_{0}>0$ such that $c_{0}t<a(t)<C_{0}t$ . Take $c\in(0,\frac{1}{2})$ and $r,R>0$ such that $cC_{0}<r<R<\frac{1}{2}c_{0}$ . Let $\Phi\in C^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{3})$ be such that

$$ 0\leq\Phi\leq 1,\quad\text{supp }\Phi\subset B_{R},\quad\Phi=1\text{ in }B_{r},\quad|\nabla\Phi|\leq C\sqrt{1-\Phi}. $$

Here, the last property can be satisfied by taking $\Phi_{0}$ satisfying the other properties and setting $\Phi=1-(1-\Phi_{0})^{2}$ . Then we define

$$ \varphi_{j}(t,x)=\Phi^{2}\Big(\frac{x-\alpha_{j}(t)}{t}\Big),\quad j=1,2,\cdots,m-1, $$

and

$$ \varphi_{m}(t,x)=1-\sum_{j=1}^{m-1}\varphi_{j}(t,x). $$

We claim that (4.31) holds. Only the estimates on $\varphi_{m}$ need to be checked.

We have $\varphi_{m}\in[0,1]$ because $\text{supp }\varphi_{j}$ are pairwise disjoint. The derivatives of $\sqrt{\varphi_{m}}$ are bounded because of the last property of $\Phi$ . ∎

Combining the properties of the cutoff functions and (2.22), we have

$$ |\varphi_{j}R-R_{j}|\leq C_{N}e^{-ca(t)},\quad\forall t>0,\ x\in\mathbb{R}^{3}. $$

This means $\varphi_{j}$ localizes the multisoliton solutions.

Consider the sum of truncated conserved quantities of the Hartree equation

$$ \displaystyle\mathcal{E}(u)= \displaystyle\int|\nabla u|^{2}-\frac{1}{2}\int\left|\nabla\phi_{|u|^{2}}\right|^{2} \displaystyle+\sum_{j=1}^{m}\bigg[\Big(\frac{1}{\lambda_{j}^{2}}+|\beta_{j}|^{2}\Big)\int\varphi_{j}|u|^{2}-2\beta_{j}\int\varphi_{j}\mathrm{Im}(\nabla u\overline{u})\bigg]. $$

By the decomposition $u=R+\varepsilon$ , we can expand $\mathcal{E}$ in terms of $\varepsilon$ . Then the second or higher order terms is $\mathcal{G}(\varepsilon)=\mathcal{G}_{1}+\mathcal{G}_{2}+\mathcal{G}_{3}$ , where

$$ \displaystyle\mathcal{G}_{1}=\int|\nabla\varepsilon|^{2}+\int\phi_{|R|^{2}}|\varepsilon|^{2}-2\int|\nabla\phi_{\mathrm{Re}(\varepsilon\overline{R})}|^{2}+2\int\phi_{\mathrm{Re}(\varepsilon\overline{R})}|\varepsilon|^{2}-\frac{1}{2}\int|\nabla\phi_{|\varepsilon|^{2}}|^{2}, \displaystyle\mathcal{G}_{2}=\sum_{j=1}^{m}\Big(\frac{1}{\lambda_{j}^{2}}+|\beta_{j}|^{2}\Big)\int\varphi_{j}|\varepsilon|^{2},\qquad\mathcal{G}_{3}=-2\sum_{j=1}^{m}\beta_{j}\int\varphi_{j}\mathrm{Im}(\nabla\varepsilon\overline{\varepsilon}). $$

We point out that because of the orthogonality condition (3.27), the first order term of $\varepsilon$ would vanish if $R$ solved (1.4). Unfortunately, as $R$ is an approximate solution, it does not solve (1.4), and the error is too big so that one cannot proceed in this way.

Therefore, we will directly prove the following two estimates on $\mathcal{G}$ . The first one states the positiveness of $\mathcal{G}$ , which follows because of orthogonality (3.27). The second follows by a direct calculation and gives an estimate on the upper bound of $\mathcal{G}$ .

#### Proposition 4.2.

Let $N\geq 2$ . For $T_{0}=T_{0}(N)$ large enough, there exists $c_{0}>0$ such that

$$ \mathcal{G}(\varepsilon(t))\geq c_{0}\|\varepsilon\|_{H^{1}}^{2},\quad\forall t\in[T_{*},T_{n}]. $$

#### Proposition 4.3.

Let $N\geq 2$ . For $T_{0}=T_{0}(N)$ large enough, if (3.34) holds, then there exists $C>0$ such that

$$ \left|\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\mathcal{G}(\varepsilon(t))\right|\leq Ct^{-1-\frac{N}{2}},\quad\forall t\in[T_{*},T_{n}]. $$

If taking these two results for granted, then by (3.28), we have

$$ c_{0}\|\varepsilon\|_{H^{1}}^{2}\leq|\mathcal{G}(\varepsilon(t))|\leq\int_{t}^{T_{n}}C\tau^{-1-\frac{N}{2}}\mathrm{d}\tau\leq\frac{C}{N}t^{-\frac{N}{2}}. $$

Taking $N$ large enough, then we obtain the first line of (3.35).

The rest of this subsection is for the proof of the two propositions. Once they are proved, we will have completed the proof of the hyperbolic case.

#### Proof of Proposition 4.2.

The main ingredient of the proof is the following coercivity result on the linearized operators $L_{-}$ and $L_{+}$ .

#### Lemma 4.4.

There exist $\delta,c>0$ such that: if $v\in H^{1}$ is real-valued, then

$$ \begin{gathered}|(v,Q)|+|(v,xQ)|<\delta\|v\|_{H^{1}}\implies(L_{+}v,v)\geq c\|v\|_{H^{1}}^{2},\\
|(v,\Lambda Q)|<\delta\|v\|_{H^{1}}\implies(L_{-}v,v)\geq c\|v\|_{H^{1}}^{2}.\end{gathered} $$

#### Proof.

All functions in this proof are assumed to be real-valued.

It suffices to prove that for some $c>0$ , if $v\in H^{1}$ , then

$$ \begin{gathered}(v,Q)=(v,xQ)=0\implies(L_{+}v,v)\geq c\|v\|_{H^{1}}^{2},\\
(v,\Lambda Q)=0\implies(L_{-}v,v)\geq c\|v\|_{H^{1}}^{2}.\end{gathered} $$

Let us only prove the sufficiency for the estimate on $L_{+}$ . For $v\in H^{1}$ , we have

$$ (L_{+}v,v)=\int|\nabla v|^{2}+\int|v|^{2}+\int\phi_{Q^{2}}v^{2}-2\int|\nabla\phi_{Qv}|^{2}. $$

If $u=v-w$ , then by the Sobolev inequality, we have

$$ (L_{+}v,v)-(L_{+}u,u)\geq-C\|u\|_{H^{1}}\|w\|_{H^{1}}-C\|w\|_{H^{1}}^{2}. $$

We take

$$ w=\frac{(v,Q)}{\|Q\|_{L^{2}}^{2}}Q+\frac{(v,xQ)}{\|xQ\|_{L^{2}}^{2}}\cdot xQ. $$

Then $\|w\|_{H^{1}}\leq C\delta\|v\|_{H^{1}}$ , and $u$ is orthogonal to both $Q$ and $xQ$ , so we have $(L_{+}u,u)\geq c\|u\|_{H^{1}}^{2}$ . We thus deduce $(L_{+}v,v)\geq\frac{c}{2}\|v\|_{H^{1}}^{2}$ by Cauchy-Schwarz and taking $\delta$ small.

We then turn to prove (4.41). We only prove the first line, as the proof of the second line is similar and easier.

Recall that $Q$ is a minimizer of

$$ \mathcal{H}(u)=\frac{1}{2}\int|\nabla u|^{2}-\frac{1}{4}\int|\nabla\phi_{|u|^{2}}|^{2},\quad\text{where }u\in H^{1}\text{ and }\|u\|_{L^{2}}=\|Q\|_{L^{2}}. $$

Thus, $Q$ is a minimizer in $H^{1}\backslash\{0\}$ of

$$ \mathcal{J}(u):=\frac{\|Q\|_{L^{2}}^{2}}{\|u\|_{L^{2}}^{2}}\int|\nabla u|^{2}-\frac{\|Q\|_{L^{2}}^{4}}{2\|u\|_{L^{2}}^{4}}\int|\nabla\phi_{|u|^{2}}|^{2}. $$

Assume $f\in H^{1}$ and $(f,Q)=0$ . By direct computation, we have

$$ \displaystyle\frac{1}{2}\frac{\mathrm{d}^{2}}{\mathrm{d}\epsilon^{2}}\bigg|_{\epsilon=0}\mathcal{J}(Q+\epsilon f)= \displaystyle\int|\nabla f|^{2}-\frac{\|\nabla Q\|_{L^{2}}^{2}}{\|Q\|_{L^{2}}^{2}}\int f^{2} \displaystyle-2\int|\nabla\phi_{Qf}|^{2}-\int\nabla\phi_{Q^{2}}\cdot\nabla\phi_{f^{2}}+\frac{\|\nabla\phi_{Q^{2}}\|_{L^{2}}^{2}}{\|Q\|_{L^{2}}^{2}}\int f^{2}. $$

Using (1.4) and integration by parts, we get

$$ \|\nabla Q\|_{L^{2}}^{2}-\|\nabla\phi_{Q^{2}}\|_{L^{2}}^{2}+\|Q\|_{L^{2}}^{2}=0. $$

Thus we obtain

$$ \frac{1}{2}\frac{\mathrm{d}^{2}}{\mathrm{d}\epsilon^{2}}\bigg|_{\epsilon=0}\mathcal{J}(Q+\epsilon f)=(L_{+}f,f). $$

By the minimality of $\mathcal{J}(Q)$ , we deduce that

$$ f\in H^{1},\ (f,Q)=0\implies(L_{+}f,f)\geq 0. $$

Therefore, if the conclusion fails to be true, then there exist $f_{n}\in H^{1}$ such that $(f_{n},Q)=(f_{n},xQ)=0$ , $\|f_{n}\|_{H^{1}}=1$ and $(L_{+}f_{n},f_{n})\to 0$ . By passing to subsequence, we may assume $f_{n}\rightharpoonup f_{0}$ in $H^{1}$ . We have $(f_{0},Q)=(f_{0},xQ)=0$ , and by the Rellich-Kondrachov theorem and the decay of $Q$ , we have

$$ \int\phi_{Q^{2}}f_{n}^{2}\to\int\phi_{Q^{2}}f_{0}^{2}\quad\text{and}\quad\int|\nabla\phi_{Qf_{n}}|^{2}\to\int|\nabla\phi_{Qf_{0}}|^{2}. $$

On the other hand, $\|f_{0}\|_{H^{1}}\leq\liminf\|f_{n}\|_{H^{1}}$ . We deduce that $(L_{+}f_{0},f_{0})\leq 0$ .

By the non-negativity of $L^{+}$ on $Q^{\perp}$ , we know that $f_{0}$ is a nonzero minimizer of $(L_{+}u,u)$ , where $u\in H^{1}$ and $(u,Q)=0$ . By computing the first variation, we get

$$ L_{+}f_{0}=aQ\quad\text{for some }a\in\mathbb{R}. $$

Since $L_{+}(\Lambda Q)=-2Q$ and $\ker L_{+}$ is spanned by $\nabla Q$ (Theorem 4 in [9]), we know $f_{0}$ is a linear combination of $\Lambda Q$ and $\nabla Q$ . But using $(f_{0},Q)=(f_{0},xQ)=0$ , we must have $f_{0}=0$ , which is a contradiction. ∎

Let $\varepsilon_{j}=\varepsilon\sqrt{\varphi_{j}}$ and $\tilde{\varepsilon}_{j}=g_{j}^{-1}\varepsilon_{j}$ , or more precisely, define

$$ \tilde{\varepsilon}_{j}(t,y_{j})=\lambda_{j}^{2}(t)\varepsilon_{j}(t,\lambda_{j}(t)y_{j}+\alpha_{j}(t))e^{i\gamma_{j}(t)-i\beta_{j}(t)\cdot(\lambda_{j}(t)y_{j}+\alpha_{j}(t))}. $$

By (3.27), (2.22) and (4.4), for $t$ large enough, we can apply Lemma 4.4 to $\mathrm{Re}(\tilde{\varepsilon}_{j})$ and $\mathrm{Im}(\tilde{\varepsilon}_{j})$ . Thus for $T_{0}(N)$ large enough, we have

$$ \Big(L_{+}\mathrm{Re}(\tilde{\varepsilon}_{j}),\mathrm{Re}(\tilde{\varepsilon}_{j})\Big)+\Big(L_{-}\mathrm{Im}(\tilde{\varepsilon}_{j}),\mathrm{Im}(\tilde{\varepsilon}_{j})\Big)\geq c\|\tilde{\varepsilon}_{j}\|_{H^{1}}^{2},\quad\forall t\geq T_{0}. $$

In the following, we always assume $T_{0}$ is large enough so that the above holds.

Set $Q_{j}=g_{j}Q$ . By computation similar to (2.4) and (2.22), we have

$$ \displaystyle\Big(L_{+}\mathrm{Re}(\tilde{\varepsilon}_{j}),\mathrm{Re}(\tilde{\varepsilon}_{j})\Big)+\Big(L_{-}\mathrm{Im}(\tilde{\varepsilon}_{j}),\mathrm{Im}(\tilde{\varepsilon}_{j})\Big) \displaystyle= \displaystyle\int|\nabla\tilde{\varepsilon}_{j}|^{2}+\int|\tilde{\varepsilon}_{j}|^{2}+\int\phi_{Q^{2}}|\tilde{\varepsilon}_{j}|^{2}+2\int\phi_{\mathrm{Re}(Q\tilde{\varepsilon}_{j})}\mathrm{Re}(Q\tilde{\varepsilon}_{j}) \displaystyle= \displaystyle\lambda_{j}^{3}\left(\int|\nabla\varepsilon_{j}|^{2}-2\beta_{j}\int\mathrm{Im}(\nabla\varepsilon_{j}\overline{\varepsilon_{j}})+|\beta_{j}|^{2}\int|\varepsilon_{j}|^{2}\right)+\lambda_{j}\int|\varepsilon_{j}|^{2} \displaystyle+\lambda_{j}^{3}\int\phi_{Q_{j}^{2}}|\varepsilon_{j}|^{2}+2\lambda_{j}^{3}\int\phi_{\mathrm{Re}(\varepsilon_{j}\overline{Q_{j}})}\mathrm{Re}(\varepsilon\overline{Q_{j}}) \displaystyle= \displaystyle\lambda_{j}^{3}\Bigg(\int|\nabla\varepsilon_{j}|^{2}+\int\phi_{|R_{j}|^{2}}|\varepsilon_{j}|^{2}-2\int\big|\nabla\phi_{\mathrm{Re}(\varepsilon_{j}\overline{{R_{j}}})}\big|^{2} \displaystyle+\Big(\frac{1}{\lambda_{j}^{2}}+|\beta_{j}|^{2}\Big)\int|\varepsilon_{j}|^{2}-2\beta_{j}\int\mathrm{Im}(\nabla\varepsilon_{j}\overline{\varepsilon_{j}})\Bigg)+O_{N}\left(\frac{\|\varepsilon_{j}\|_{H^{1}}^{2}}{a}\right) $$

We then deduce that

$$ \mathcal{H}_{j}(\varepsilon_{j})\geq c\|\varepsilon_{j}\|_{H^{1}}-\frac{C_{N}}{a}\|\varepsilon_{j}\|_{H^{1}}^{2}\geq c\int\varphi_{j}(|\nabla\varepsilon|^{2}+|\varepsilon|^{2})-\frac{C_{N}}{a}\|\varepsilon\|_{H^{1}}^{2}, $$

where

$$ \displaystyle\mathcal{H}_{j}(\varepsilon_{j})= \displaystyle\int|\nabla\varepsilon_{j}|^{2}+\int\phi_{|R_{j}|^{2}}|\varepsilon_{j}|^{2}-2\int\big|\nabla\phi_{\mathrm{Re}(\varepsilon_{j}\overline{{R_{j}}})}\big|^{2} \displaystyle+\Big(\frac{1}{\lambda_{j}^{2}}+|\beta_{j}|^{2}\Big)\int|\varepsilon_{j}|^{2}-2\beta_{j}\int\mathrm{Im}(\nabla\varepsilon_{j}\overline{\varepsilon_{j}}). $$

Next, we consider the truncated functional

$$ \displaystyle\mathcal{H}_{j,\varphi}(\varepsilon)= \displaystyle\int\varphi_{j}|\nabla\varepsilon|^{2}+\int\phi_{|R_{j}|^{2}}|\varepsilon|^{2}-2\int\big|\nabla\phi_{\mathrm{Re}(\varepsilon\overline{{R_{j}}})}\big|^{2} \displaystyle+\Big(\frac{1}{\lambda_{j}^{2}}+|\beta_{j}|^{2}\Big)\int\varphi_{j}|\varepsilon|^{2}-2\beta_{j}\int\varphi_{j}\mathrm{Im}(\nabla\varepsilon\overline{\varepsilon}). $$

By (4.31), (4.35) and (4.56), we have

$$ \displaystyle\mathcal{H}_{j,\varphi}(\varepsilon)= \displaystyle\int|\nabla\varepsilon_{j}|^{2}+\int\phi_{|R_{j}|^{2}}|\varepsilon|^{2}-2\int\big|\nabla\phi_{\mathrm{Re}(\varepsilon\overline{{R_{j}}})}\big|^{2} \displaystyle+\Big(\frac{1}{\lambda_{j}^{2}}+|\beta_{j}|^{2}\Big)\int|\varepsilon_{j}|^{2}-2\beta_{j}\int\mathrm{Im}(\nabla\varepsilon_{j}\overline{\varepsilon_{j}})+O\left(\frac{\|\varepsilon\|_{H^{1}}^{2}}{a}\right) \displaystyle= \displaystyle\mathcal{H}_{j}(\varepsilon_{j})+\int(1-\sqrt{\varphi_{j}})\phi_{|R_{j}|^{2}}|\varepsilon|^{2}-2\int\big|\nabla\phi_{\mathrm{Re}\big((1-\sqrt{\varphi_{j}})\varepsilon R_{j}\big)}\big|^{2} \displaystyle+4\int\phi_{\mathrm{Re}(\varepsilon_{j}R_{j})}\mathrm{Re}\big((1-\sqrt{\varphi_{j}})\varepsilon R_{j}\big)+O\left(\frac{\|\varepsilon\|_{H^{1}}^{2}}{a}\right) \displaystyle\geq \displaystyle c\int\varphi_{j}(|\nabla\varepsilon|^{2}+|\varepsilon|^{2})-\frac{C_{N}}{a}\|\varepsilon\|_{H^{1}}^{2}. $$

Finally, using the sum-to-1 property of $\varphi_{j}$ , we write

$$ \displaystyle\mathcal{G}(\varepsilon)= \displaystyle\sum_{j=1}^{m}\mathcal{H}_{j,\varphi}(\varepsilon)+2\int\phi_{\mathrm{Re}(\varepsilon\overline{R})}|\varepsilon|^{2}-\frac{1}{2}\int|\nabla\phi_{|\varepsilon|^{2}}|^{2} \displaystyle+\sum_{j\neq k}\int\phi_{\mathrm{Re}(R_{k}\overline{R_{j}})}|\varepsilon|^{2}-2\sum_{j\neq k}\int\nabla\phi_{\mathrm{Re}(\varepsilon\overline{R_{j}})}\cdot\nabla\phi_{\mathrm{Re}(\varepsilon\overline{R_{k}})}. $$

The first term is controlled by (4.59). The other terms in the first line are $O\big(t^{-N/4}\|\varepsilon\|_{H^{1}}^{2}\big)$ because of (3.34). Using Lemma 2.5, we know the two terms in the second line are $O_{N}\big(e^{-ca}\|\varepsilon\|_{H^{1}}^{2}\big)$ and $O_{N}\Big(\frac{\|\varepsilon\|_{H^{1}}^{2}}{a}\Big)$ , respectively. We thus have

$$ \mathcal{G}(\varepsilon)\geq c\|\varepsilon\|_{H^{1}}^{2}-\frac{C_{N}}{a}\|\varepsilon\|_{H^{1}}^{2}. $$

Thanks to (4.4), we conclude by taking $T_{0}(N)$ large enough. ∎
